en: Padmagupta (also known as Parimala):
*Navasāhasāṅkacarita* First Canto (Prathamaḥ Sargaḥ)
May that moon protect you, whose naturally curved form mimics the play of the strung bow of Cupid,
its two ends licked by the rays of the jewels from the king of serpents bound within his matted locks.

May that moon—the crest-jewel upon the head of Śaṅkara—protect you; it is pale-red with the luster of the jewels in his matted locks, and whom the Daughter of the Mountain King desires to make into an ear-ornament out of curiosity for the sprouts of the Aśoka tree.
May the temple of the Jar-born (Ganesha) protect you— its ground strewn with vermilion powder,
appearing like the sprouting rays of the morning sun spat forth for the pacification of the swarms of darkness that are obstacles.
May that eternal eye of Sarasvatī, which opens forever before your mouths, be manifest;
for by it the lords of poets, being attentive, behold the reality existing within the triple heaven.
Praise of Ancient Poets: Victorious are those ancient poets who touched upon ultimate reality, headed by the illustrious Bhartṛmeṇṭha;
for their words proceeded along the Vaidarbha path, which is like the edge of a sharp sword.

The glories of those who travel along the path revealed by the eloquent instructions of the great poets, such as Bhartṛmeṇṭha and others, are more beautiful even than the orb of the full moon, standing not far before them. (PNc 1.6)
We pay homage to King Vākpatirāja, the single bulbous root of the Sarasvatī-kalpalatā,
by whose grace we too may travel upon the path trodden by no other lord of poets.
That seal which Vākpatirājadeva, desiring to go to heaven, placed upon my speech—
that very seal Sindhurāja, the younger brother of that friend of poets, now breaks.
"Shyness and such traits belong to the novice poet;

how many of these lords of poets are there in the composition of poetry? Is this why I have been appointed by the King? Or rather, is a sandhill being piled up while the noble mountains exist? (PNc 1.9)
Oh, how great is this audacity that the Navasāhasāṅka is even to be described! For the talk of delimiting his virtues is far away, like that of the waters of the ocean. (PNc 1.10)
Or rather, through devotion to this very work of mine, this subtle spark of power unfolds;
for that the ocean was leaped over by the monkey is the fruit of the service rendered to the scion of Raghu.
In the envious hearts of the wicked, the quality of well-spoken words never leads to virtue;
it is as futile as a decorative pattern of saffron on the naturally dark cheek of Indra’s consort.
What else remains for me to say of this king, who is adorned by deeds as pure as pearls?
Let the naturally pure minds of the virtuous close like buds at my words.
Homage be to that essence of literary art (sāhityarasa), by even a single drop of which infused within,
the face of the virtuous attains a golden luster, while that of the wicked turns to a foul color.
Or rather, whose hearts do my words not captivate, for they are pregnant with the radiant glory of the illustrious King Sāhasāṅka?
For to whom would those oysters not be a source of longing, within whose bellies pearls gleam?
Behold now, my vow: these Parijata flowers born of the Lord of Avanti, white as the moon, the lord of stars.
I shall fashion the flowers of fame of the brides of the quarters into ear-ornaments.
Now follows the description of Ujjayinī:
There is on earth a city named Ujjayinī, like Amarāvatī in the sky;
in it took up his residence the lord of the earth, Śrī Vikramāditya, who was equal to Indra. (PNc 1.17)
On its slope, the moat shines like a girdle of resonant gold, tawny with the pollen of blooming lotuses and the murmuring of rows of swans.
There, under the guise of a rampart and a moat, the body of Murāri encircles his couch of play,
like the lord of serpents who has emerged from the depths to guard the treasure situated within.
That city, which at every step supports the dwellings of the gods— resplendent with thick, pure white plaster—
as if it were the glory of the kings that had risen up to fill the realm of the Lord of Serpents.

In that city, the nets of pearls suspended as pendants seem to mock one another with their webs of rays, which steal the brilliance of falling flakes of snow, acting as the playful pavilions for amorous women.

In that city, the houses were filled with excellent women; these noble ladies possessed limbs pre-eminent for their beauty, and their beauty was characterized by fully blossomed grace—a grace that served as the very weapon of the flower-armed god of love.
CF. *Kāvyaprakāśa* 10.131a:
Where the row of crystal windows attains the splendor of the faces of the deer-eyed women, like the braid of water from the celestial Gaṅgā adorned with lotuses fashioned of bright gold. (PNc_1.23)
In that city, the victory banners— red and made of sapphire— fluttering in the wind,
possess the brilliance of streaks of lightning rising from clouds dark as crushed collyrium.
There, in every house, the sound of the jeweled girdles of beautiful women rises repeatedly;
it serves as the festive drum-roll for the intoxicated descent of the elephant of the Conqueror of Cupid.

In that city, the moon, though situated very close to the windows, does not undergo waning even during the dark fortnight, for it has shared its splendor with the loveliness of the cheeks of the courtesans through their moon-like faces.
I do not speak this truth out of partiality, but because in the courtyards of the houses at dawn,
the pearls from single-strand necklaces are swept away by brooms.
Upon the slope of the breasts of those with expansive vision, a decorative vine of musk shines forth,
appearing like a leathern thong released by the fish-bannered god when his practice of drawing the bow was completed.

On the fringes of the fluttering banners in the mansions of the playful women, the city constantly proclaims, as it were, the command of the God of Love through the incessant jingling of golden bells.
In the festive revelries of Love’s amorous quarrels, where garments slip away at every moment,
it is as if the smoke from the abundant black aloe-wood incense bestows a fresh garment upon the fair-browed women.

There, in the palaces, women with curling hair complete the half-moons— whose beauty was incomplete as they approached the eighth-day moon— by filling them with the inner feathers of *ketaka* flowers gathered from their locks.
In whose *aśoka* tree-lined avenues the flower-bowed god, having fixed the flash of his enchanting weapon within the playful side-glances of those with intoxicating eyes, sports together with Rati.

I know that in that city, out of the world-enchanting curiosity of the Creator, cuckoos— having made their warbling a mere pretext— study day and night in the mango groves the science of the arrows of Love.
Under the guise of the shafts of light wandering through the circle of the quarters,
I perceive that [the city] appoints the golden archways to hold the golden staffs after having conquered the cities of the world-protectors.

In the palace where rows of golden windows were radiant, the front altar shone with the clusters of crystal rays as they swayed upon the staff-like shafts of light, appearing as if it were being fanned by shimmering, brilliant chowries.

In that city, the sky always shines as if embraced by the twilight glow, rosy with the mass of rays from the rubies in the courtyards of the houses, and possessing a crimson luster like that of *kiṃśuka* flowers.

Having reached that city, where every day the young male swans cast upon the fair-browed women the suspicion that they were green pigeons— due to their friendship with the rays of the clear vaidūrya-jewel staircases in the palace ponds.

There, the playful lovers have no need for mirrors when they gaze upon the beauty of their own faces, as they are fully satisfied by the bright cheeks of young women that resemble the orb of the moon.

In that city, young men suddenly perceive feigned anger in the deer-eyed women upon seeing their faces reflected in jeweled walls, even when those women have turned away from them, as if they were looking at a palace.

In that city, young women— whose cheeks are streaked by the dark aloe-wood patterns painted upon them— cause the water in the palace ponds to become mottled with droplets of perspiration breaking forth from the fatigue of their amorous play with the flower-arrowed god.

In them there blossoms a certain extraordinary splendor of good fortune belonging to beautiful women, for that which is like a string of pearls of grace always remains close to their necks, dear to them.
I know that when the deer are lured away by the songs of the women standing upon the roofs of the mansions,
the moon in that city assumes the likeness of their bright, round cheeks against the dark night.
She has attained renown everywhere as "Durgā" (the one who goes with difficulty), like the daughter of the mountain king accompanied by Nīlakaṇṭha;
she possesses an exceeding splendor through her girdle fastened upon her waist and her lion-throne.
With the fragrant blossoms of the trees along its banks scattered by the wind from their stalks,
the Śiprā river— dark as a tamāla tree on its bank— shines like the braid of hair of that city.
Enveloped on all sides by smoke issuing from many mouths,
she shone as if obstructed by the great ocean out of envy, thinking, "She is a jewel more excellent than myself."
In that city, the lotus-eyes of the graceful women overstep the path of the Vedas;
yet even there, only the crescent moon in the matted locks of Mahākāla bears a crookedness.

In that city, even the pavilion of Caṇḍī’s husband bears the appearance of a peacock-feather parasol, as it is covered by a multitude of many-colored jeweled cloths hanging down from the tips of its banners and suspended in the sky.
In ancient times, it is said, that portion of Brahmā’s water-pot which was filled with most meritorious waters—
those very waters the Destroyer of Tripura bears here upon the region of his hip like a mirror.
In that city, where rows of many celestial mansions stand, the rays radiating from the tops of their jeweled banners paint, as it were,
variegated patterns upon the breasts of the immortal women.

In which, at dawn, the vine-cottages in the gardens on the banks of the Śiprā indicate the trysting places of young men by means of discarded girdles and the whistling sounds produced by the whirling of whisks.

In that city, the garden grounds shine with golden pleasure-mountains adorned with sandalwood and the dense, wafting fragrance of musk, enchanting those filled with desire, as if they were the breasts of the land itself.
When the city’s playful women hurriedly reached the bank because of the buffeting by a timingila fish,
the Śiprā river there shone as if with a moist smile of pearls under the guise of her shimmering mass of foam.

In that city, clouds, having come into contact with the agallochum incense smoke from the pleasure-chambers of wanton women and having taken up residence upon the turrets of the palaces, discharge fragrant water.

In that city, where the beauty of the waves was illuminated by excellent lotuses and the sound of mṛdaṅga drums was played incessantly, gazelle-eyed women took delight in the dance-halls as if they were the waters of a garden pond.
In that city, during the dark nights when the masses of darkness on the streets were dispelled by the lattice of light from ruby windows,
young women with trembling breasts would somehow reach their secret trysts.

There, during the rainy season, the footprints of the celestial beauties, marked with red lac, become visible upon the high palace floors of ruddy jewels that reflect the likeness of fresh rain clouds.
I believe that she, the jewel of the middle world, was fashioned here by the Creator with the utmost concentration,
as if to manifest the supreme excellence of his own artistic knowledge.
Now, the description of the hero:
In that city there was a king named Sindhurāja, whose waves of fame rested in the groves of the lordly Kulācala mountains;
he was like the sun among the planets, having attained preeminence at the head of all monarchs.
He who had accomplished various wonderful feats of valor and was himself embraced by Fortune in battle—
whom some call by the name Navasāhasāṅka, while others call him Kumāranārāyaṇa.
By him of vast prowess, who effortlessly rescued the earth submerged in the fathomless ocean of his enemies,
the primordial sport of the Primeval Boar was made manifest here in this world.

On him, whose laughter is like the waves of the surging Ocean of Milk, the breasts of his enemies' wives abandon their pearl necklaces as if out of fear of being stained by the mud of falling tears mixed with collyrium.
The blade of his sword, wondrously acquiring the touch of hands instantly in battle after battle, shone with radiance.
From her, who is dark as the *tāla* tree, is born a fame, white as the autumn moon, which serves as an ornament for the three worlds.
Even though her husband was always turned away from the property of others, alas, the stainless fame of former kings has been forcibly plundered by him, [the fame] of the earth girdled by the oceans!
Serene mind, dignity, majesty, valor, and the earth—these, along with truth and Sarasvatī herself, reside upon his lotus-like face; this is indeed the case for only two such persons.
Hearing the detailed account of his triumphs over his arms being sung by the Apsarases,
Indra’s body— seeming to receive the touch of Śacī’s breasts— becomes covered with horripilation.
And by him, even in his youth, these four things were accomplished through four qualities:
wisdom was perfected by learning, sovereignty by statesmanship, fortune by generosity, and the earth by his power.
In battle after battle, that master of weapons, casting aside all pity,
whetted his sharp-edged sword upon the surfaces of the emerald-grinding stones that were the rubies from the crowns of the gathered hosts of many kings.
By the weight of the earth clearly bowing down, the masses of dust from the jewels on the hoods of Śeṣa closed the lotus-eyes of the serpent maidens during his victorious expedition.
In whose courtyards, during the audiences of kings, the women of the harem stumble upon heaps of pearls scattered there by necklaces that have snapped asunder from mutual entanglement.

By him, who has made *guñjā* berries into ornaments upon the orb of the breasts of his enemies' wives— berries which, by displacing their pearl necklaces, evoke the suspicion that they are sparks from the fire of his own prowess.

In the forefront of battle, the clouds of dust rising from the pearls bursting from the frontal globes of the lordly elephants of his enemies— shattered by the falling strokes of his sword— make his fame grow ever more substantial.

That enemy, whose splendor was like the moon, by whom a single-string necklace— white as a kunda flower, a banner of victory for the festival of the bodiless god of love— and a woman with lovely eyes were both driven far away from his neck.
Upon him, whose long arms— darkened by the calluses of the bowstring— sustain the earth bounded by the ocean,
the waist of the women of the Paurava clan appears as the supreme abode of poverty.

He who, with the tip of his sword made crimson by weapons, seized his own kingdom in battle— its king, the lord of Kuntala, having been obscured by the dense darkness that pervaded the circle of the quarters— just as the sun, with its orb reddened by its rays, takes back the day when it is hidden within thick gloom.
By his exceedingly right arm, which shook them like the wind,
there arose upon the battlefield a shower of teardrop-blossoms from the creepers that were the wives of his enemies.
With her eyebrows, which were intensely curved and flashing as they shattered the hearts of his adversaries,
that scorcher of enemies did not merely assume the form of a bow, but was emulated even in action.
Having reached that sandalwood tree which was his body, the supreme glory of the enemy kings— possessing flowers of shimmering and dense fame—
attained great growth like a *lavalī* creeper firmly rooted there.
He who suddenly grants safety from fear to his enemies who have bowed down before him receives fame as white as the powder of snow,
pearl necklaces, lotus stalks, and camphor.
They say that the rising of this treasury of light brings hope to all creatures on every side,
while the eyes of the wives of his enemies are enveloped by the darkness of collyrium-like tears.
At whose departure, by the weight of his army, the earth— whose seal is the seven oceans—
trembles upon the hoods of the serpent-king, which are crowded with the mutual friction [of their scales].

People throughout the three worlds speak of him— who is delightful with his long virtues and whose emotions are clearly manifest— as the single bow of the flower-armed god that surpasses the pride of the lotus-eyed women.
Without a doubt, the Creator first fashioned him alone as the sole benefactor of the three worlds;
thereafter, he created the wish-fulfilling trees and other such things from the remaining fragments of his atoms.
The fame of that lord, white as the pale leaves of a ripened *tāla* fruit, arises from his unfeigned generosity and forms clusters upon the circles of the creepers of the quarters.
In him, whose feet were kissed by the luster of the jewels in the crowns of the circle of kings subdued by his majesty and vigor,
and who possessed a prowess equal to that of Yayāti, Pāṇḍu, and Dilīpa, the title of "King" attained its true meaning.

He by whom the free-roaming elephant of the Kali age was forcibly restrained— as if by a goad— while it plunged into the lake of the earth and ravaged the groves of lotuses that are the acts of righteousness.
[VAR 1.85c: {of the elephant of the Kali age / lem / ed;
of the elephant of sin /}]

Wherever those various virtues— shining like white water-lilies, the moon, and jasmine— though long separated and complete in themselves, come together in one place as if out of curiosity for the happiness of dwelling together.
The circles of the breasts of the wives of his enemies, though smeared with saffron, appear as if anointed with the beauty of eyes reddened by excessive weeping.
In fortune, majesty, fame, forbearance, generosity, elegance, humility, and greatness—to what else could he be compared? Neither Rantideva, nor Pṛthu, nor Pārtha attained such equality as he.
Regarding the description of his ministers: he has a minister named Yaśobhaṭa, who is bold enough to bear the burden of imperial sovereignty;
whom poets call Ramāṅgada by another name because of the practice of his own excellent compositions.
Having conquered even Laṅkā, that city which exists remains beyond comparison even with Alakā;
there is another city of that conqueror, his family capital, known by the name Dhārā.
Upon her,
that Lord— whose golden footstool is made to sprout by the rays from the crest-jewels of kings conquered by his valor—
enjoys this circle of the earth, which easily serves as an ornament for his single, upraised parasol of grace.

Thus ends the first canto, titled "Description of the City and the King," in the epic poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* composed by Padmagupta— also known by the name Parimala— the son of the illustrious Mṛgāṅkagupta.
The second canto: Once, having become the guest of his eyes in a painted chamber,
that king was intensely moved by the hunt depicted therein.
Mounted upon a spirited horse, together with the princes,
he whose commands were never in vain proceeded from the mountain to the forest of the Vindhya.
With his hair held back by a necklace of large, pure pearls,
he acquired the splendor of Lord Dhūrjaṭi, whose topknot is bound by the king of serpents.
That god, with his armor resembling a lotus leaf and girt with dark clouds, shone like a mountain of gold.
Above him, O Lord, a blue parasol shone resplendently,
like a dark mass of clouds over the yellow waters of the ocean.
Shaken by the wind released from the fan,
that chowrie shone like the sighs of the former kings escaping from the prison of their captors for the sake of his glory.
[VAR 2.6a: {vyādhūti/lem / ed (not attested); c: {gṛhāt/lem /}
With the rays of the crest-jewels rising high as if from a wound,
he cast a noose for the deer of the night-maker upon the path of the sky.
Upon the shoulders of that Man-Lion, the mass of manes, radiant with the luster of his necklaces, bore the beauty of the playful smiles of the Goddess Śrī clinging to his throat.
Before him, at every step, the radiance of the various jeweled armlets of that Prācīnabarhis created a moving bow.
Enveloped by the luster of the rubies in his neck-ornament,
he shone like another Bhārgava who had just bathed in the lake of the blood of kings.
He shone forth, preceded by a succession of white parasols,
like the lord of the waters with foam tossed up by the wind at the shore.
The wind, bearing the fragrance of the filaments of wakeful lotuses as its offering,
attended upon that sovereign like a messenger from the Vindhya mountains.
Then, from the heaps of dust kicked up by the hooves of the cavalry,
the world became once again filled with the apprehension that the Vindhya mountains were growing back by force.
White dogs with golden chains went before him,
bearing the splendor of autumnal clouds adorned with streaks of lightning.
Then, by the neighing of horses and the clamor of the foot soldiers,
the lands of the Vindhyas became filled with beasts of prey bewildered by fear.
With their eyes fixed upon his ears as if they were ear-ornaments,
the forest deities at the edge of the grove beheld him, who had violently drawn his bow, appearing like the god of love himself.
Thinking, "While I am the protector, this thief has stolen the beauty of the gazes of these helpless women," he discharged an arrow at the black antelope.
Like King Śrīharṣa, that lord of the earth brought about a union between Bāṇa and Mayūra, who were captivating with their variegated and elegant compositions.
With the tails of yaks severed by his arrows, he made the forest radiant all around, as if with clusters of the blossoms of his own fame.
As if challenged by the sounds of his tail-lashing,
he rushed forward with curiosity toward the tigers ahead of him.
Desiring to manifest his own extraordinary heroism,
he whose eyes were like white lotuses discharged arrows at the white lotuses.
As if ashamed by the sight of his prowess,
those [enemies] abandoned their rivalry in valor before him, yet they surrendered even their lives afterwards.
As if out of envy, that lord of the earth, which possessed the single umbrella of sovereignty,
could not endure the Vindhya mountain’s state of possessing lofty white lotuses.
From him, who rained down a shower of arrows, the forest buffaloes fled far away,
like darknesses scattered by the rays of the sun.
The sport of crushing the great buffalo reached its conclusion between that exceedingly fierce king and Caṇḍikā, whose conduct is fierce.
As the twang of his bow spread forth like the autumn season,
the Vindhya ocean became like a lion yawning and stretching out from sleep.
In him, whose prowess was renowned throughout the entire world,
even the beasts of prey cast sidelong glances out of pride, for his valor remained unmanifested [to them].
He could not endure the pearl-ornaments from intoxicated elephants upon the claw-shells [of his soldiers] as they moved through the streets of their innate and exalted valor.
When the herd of great boars had come within the range of his arrows,
the lineage of the lotus-roots in the pond finally attained well-being after a long time.
Out of curiosity, he made of the lions' claws torn from their muzzles patterns on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains that resembled scattered crescent moons.
Taking up his bow, he in an instant rendered the forest devoid of female camels, female deer, female boars, female lions, and female tigers.
"Enough of striking at innocent beings, O protector of the earth!"—
as if saying this, the rows of forest trees seemed to forbid him with the cries of their birds.
The breezes, kissing the garlands from the hair-tresses of Śabara women exhausted by amorous play, attended upon him whose fatigue from hunting had vanished.
Then,
with an intense passion for the hunt, he beheld a deer moving here and there, as graceful as a rainbow.
He too, having turned his neck and stood for a moment, beheld it;
then he entered the Vindhya grove, which was thick with clusters of creepers.
Then, having released the horse and dismissed his followers as well, he whose eyes were as long as a deer’s pursued that deer, he who possessed eyes as broad as a deer’s.
Then that king was followed by Ramāṅgada as if by Śrī herself;
yet the shadow of that monarch never once departed from him.
Wandering from forest to forest with his bow in hand, tracking deer, he assumed the graceful bearing of the wielder of the Pināka, who is disguised as a Kirāta.
Then, from afar, he was made a target by him with a feathered arrow,
gold-tufted and bearing his own name as its mark.
Although his grip was somewhat loosened, as he was capable of splitting stone,
that deer was pierced by him both in its hide and in its vital organ.
[The splitting of rocks; or: the opening of veins.]
Terrified by the falling of arrows, he was led to a great distance by the deer with a speed exceeding even that of the mind, like another Rāma.
Running through the middle of the Vindhya forest, amidst the dense thickets of creepers,
he was seen only as he repeatedly leapt up and up.
Then the lord of the earth beheld him as he had already traveled far away with speed, making the forest glades appear as if strewn with blue lotuses by his very glance.
Then, when he had vanished, he— his curiosity still unquenched—
attained a state of profound embarrassment upon the earth, like one’s own discharged arrow.
"Making the creepers appear as if covered in clusters of blossoms by the moonlight of his teeth," he said with a smile to Ramāṅgada, who was standing at his side.
[VAR 2.45a: {by means of moonlight}]
O Ramāṅgada,
has this deer, whose body rivals that of the lover of Paulomī’s husband [Indra], perhaps come within the range of your vision? (PNc 2.46)
Marked by the decorative leaf-patterns drawn with her own hand by his wives,
might this temple-deer belong to the charioteer of Agni?
Have you seen the golden chain around his neck,
like a flash of lightning upon a cloud streaked with Indra’s bow?
"This species of deer is unprecedented in every way upon the surface of the earth;
it could only exist on the mountain of the immortals or in the realm of the hooded serpents."
I shall place this shield, which possesses the luster of Indra’s bow and is exceedingly purifying, upon the back of my elephant during the great festivals of battle.
Since this mortal heart sinks into the waves of the flavor of curiosity,
come, let us strive to seek out its path.
When that supreme lord of men had ceased speaking thus,
Ramāṅgada, having obtained the opportunity, spoke these words.

O Lord, this beautiful deer has been pursued far by you with your strung bow, as if out of anger at seeing the mixture of colors [of its spots], just as the one who fashioned the golden armlet forbade the pursuit of the deer.
These Vindhya lands, filled with gods, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and serpents,
are ever-new treasures of wonders.
"O Viramati, why this excessive devotion of yours to the pursuit of deer?
The intellects of those like you do not run toward activities that are devoid of purpose."
As you wander here with your mind intent on hunting,
he will fall once more within the range of your eyes upon the path.
"Let this arrow be withdrawn and let the bow also be lowered;
O Lord, may the rest of the lineage of wild beasts be blessed with well-being."
This is the intense state of the day, that this blessed Sun bestows upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest the splendor of the Kaustubha gem from the sky.
O Lord, now that these beings have been slain by you, these forest lands seem as if distressed and carry an exceeding grief.
Look, here the partridges, untired by these young *vānīra* branches, suddenly take flight and vanish from sight.
Behold how the male cuckoos remain in these royal rose-apple groves, as if painted there, withered by the rays of the sun even though they are situated right here.
Look, this affectionate shade of the *nīpa* tree, a source of delight, is being enjoyed by a wild elephant who has come here of his own accord.
This rising column of smoke from the forest fire, dark as a fresh rain-cloud,
is being gazed upon with longing by peacocks here, parched with thirst.
By this gaze, tawny like a fragment of a coral stalk,
the buffalo emerging from the mud of this pond becomes clearly visible.
O King, for the royal swan now scorched by the harsh heat of the sun,
this lotus leaf serves as a parasol.
O Lord, these drops of perspiration, though their brilliance is surpassed by the surface of your cheeks covered by the king of horses' mane, now cause even your face to appear jagged with teeth.
Therefore, let this fatigue from the hunt be dispelled by you here in this bower of creepers, which is smiling with blossoms and filled with the humming of intoxicated bees.
Moreover, O Lord, this lotus pond before you has clear water and sandy banks marked by ruddy geese; its mud has been turned up by wild boars.
This breeze, shaking the buds of the *kahlāra* lilies, has been sent by her to summon you, who are exhausted by the rays of the sun.
"Let this path, strewn with clusters of vine blossoms, be traversed;
from here, these grounds are gravelly, covered by the pearls dropped by wild elephants."
When this was said, he gently placed his foot upon the king’s smile,
which rested upon the ivory seat of the jewel of Sarasvatī.
Then, having traveled a short distance along the path pointed out by Yaśobhaṭa,
that ornament of Avanti reached the bank of a lotus pond.
From his hand, whose fingers were moist with thick sweat,
his attendant took up a bow along with an arrow, as if it were the bow of the God of Love himself.
Now follows the description of his bathing and so forth:
Then, touched by the desire to bathe and having cast off his dark tunic,
he shone like the moon released from the clouds, fully restored to its splendor.
With the dust of the hunt wiped away by the person standing at his side,
his face shone like a lotus from which the pollen has been blown away by the wind.
His body, naturally graceful and free from ornaments,
became like a *pārijāta* creeper with its clusters of blossoms cast down.
As he plunged into the lake, his limbs and complexion refreshed by the sweat,
his splendor spread out to the very edges like that of a forest-dweller.
[Only in K; the edition reads:
"With his body-unguents melted by perspiration, he plunged into that lake like a wild elephant whose dust is raised by the blows of his temples drenched with rut."]
There, upon her whose girdle was the rows of birds scattered far and wide, he,
whose flower-weapon was in full bloom, sported at his pleasure.
Even under the guise of its quivering stalks and thorns,
that lotus plant bore, as it were, a thrill of horripilation at the touch of her slender body.

Description of Śaśiprabhā:
He has a daughter named Śaśiprabhā, a virtuous maiden who is the sole ornament of the world; she entered the realm of the serpents all at once, like a crescent moon entering out of fear of Rāhu.
Since she moves so extremely swiftly while wandering in her games with the ball that she cannot be overtaken by anyone,

Neither Rati, nor Śacī, nor Citralekhā, nor Ghṛtācī, nor Tilottamā, nor Rambhā possesses even a fraction of the audacity to imitate her, whose perfection of form is throbbing with wonder.
Having attained friendship with the daughters of the *suras*, *kinnaras*, and *siddhas* who were themselves devoted to the practice of their own arts, she—
possessing a sharpened intellect— reached the highest excellence in all the arts even during her childhood.

the restless pet deer of that large-eyed woman fled and went away somewhere.

overcome by exhaustion, spent the night on the sandy bank of the river born of the moon.

This effort of mine is directed toward searching for him even in these forest tracts, though they are dense with herds of black antelopes amidst dappled cows and possess ponds inhabited by rutting wild boars.

Know me to be the daughter of that lord of serpents named Hema, a maiden appointed by him to hold the white yak-tail fan; my name is Pāṭalā.
This searching of mine has borne fruit, though my exertion was well-nigh in vain,
for here in the midst of the forest you, the Supreme Person, have been seen, embraced by dense splendor.
If you do not consider this entreaty, or if you have partiality toward us, then tell us:
while wandering somewhere in this forest, have you ever seen that bird who was carried away by you?
I do not think you have seen her here either; therefore, I shall turn back from this search.
Surely that princess of the Naga king is suffering greatly with anxious thoughts as I delay.

Or rather, she— her eyes offered in love toward the arrow of the nine-thousand-armed [Śiva] brought by the Destroyer of the Deer (Śiva) according to the prescribed rite— surely remains even now as if painted, bearing his name.
Again she uttered the words "Pāṭala’s speech," and having looked at those arrows as if once more struck with wonder,
her face smiling at the memory of the arrows brought back by the deer during their sport, she spoke again.
I believe you alone are that moon of the world of men, since that arrow of yours, fixed with the intent for the hunt,
seems to correspond to those arrows of yours that grant fearlessness to the worlds.
O ornament of the earth, this mark of your name, clearly inscribed, remains upon these iron-tipped arrows;
it forcibly wipes away even the slightest trace of doubt that had taken root within me.
O moon among kings, what else could bring security to these three realms than this triad?
For by you, the enemy of Namuci, heaven has been secured; by Vāsuki, the earth; and by you, the netherworld.
While you, like Dilīpa, rule the earth as a lord of men whose commands are unbroken,
who else but that bird-thief of necklaces would set foot upon such a wicked path?
This arm of yours, marked by the scars of bowstrings, does not feel shame before the wicked for being a friend;
for while this earth was being protected by it, we were robbed by even a mere bird.
"Let the bird depart; I have no need for it, for you alone must be entreated here for the necklace. Do those who enjoy a sixth part of the earth not grant what has been stolen by a thief? PNc_5.51.
O Lord, if you stand upon the noble path established by Manu, then let that necklace be returned;
for rulers such as yourself never overstep the way of those who know what is right.
If you desire your own [true] arrow, why is it not obtainable even by you who are so diligent,
since you have committed a deception by striking the innocent deer of Śaśiprabhā’s beauty as if in sport?
Or rather, the daughter of the lord of serpents will not give up the necklace;
for once you have become a guest within the path of her vision, it will be easy for her to cause a great disturbance among the people.
From afar, this king of mountains appears like you, O proud one, towering in height;
and between him and us flows the Revā river, its banks crowded with affection by the kalahamsa geese.
That fair-bodied woman, whose face is like a sister to the digit of the nectar-moon,
stands upon the riverbank like the daughter of the Ocean-King upon the chest of the Discus-Wielder, adorned with a forest garland.

By these words of his—words that were like a spring day, the season for the joyful blossoming of the sole messenger of Love—[he was moved].
Thus the king attained an indescribable joy, like a peacock at the sound of a mass of rain clouds.

And the lord of kings, smiling, spoke to that playful daughter of the king of serpents with words as resonant as the cry of young peacocks, resembling the rumbling of fresh clouds: *avadac ca vihasya pārthivendraḥ phaṇirājendrasutāvilāsinīṃ tām / vacasotkayatā mayūraśāvān navajīmūtaninādasodareṇa //* PNc_5.59 //

yet, since these faults were committed by you, we have become guilty even for our own transgressions.

while I strive to search for her ornaments here upon the sands of this pond.

Even within the interior of the treasury, that fawn-eyed woman, overcome with wonder, beheld him with eyes whose lashes were upturned— as if he were seen by a gaze fixed in a painting, for he was difficult even for the Lord of Serpents to attain.
Having playfully drawn from his upper garment a gift of moon-like radiance, like a canopy of stars from a white cloud,
the Lord bore upon his chest the necklace resting on the couch of Śaśiprabhā’s breasts.
Then Ramāṅgada, knowing his husband’s intention, spoke laughingly to that female serpent:
"If you are curious and not envious, then look here from this place at something over there."
Then, her gaze drawn by the necklace, Pāṭalā suddenly beheld upon the king’s chest that very ornament of the daughter of the serpent-king, which had been snatched away by the flock of water-birds.
Again, Pāṭalā, bathing her lip— which possessed the splendor of a reflected bimba fruit— with the nectar-like luster of her smile,
"O Hāra, have you come here in the form of a mythical swan (rājahaṃsa) to carry me away?
You are known; indeed, there is a report that in the city of the serpents (Uragapura), one can assume any form at will."
O Lord of Men, if your mind were not so skilled in deceiving others, how else could you have taken this ornament from Śaśiprabhā in the forest— an ornament as white as the laughter of Hara?
I understand that you do not tolerate even a fraction of impropriety anywhere on the circle of the earth when you have taken up the rod of punishment;
yet, why is this—that you yourself establish your residence in a realm inhabited by bandits?
"O Lord of the Earth, why do you smile? Is this not mere sport? Give back our necklace!
Do those like you, who follow the path of policy, not feel shame here for seizing the property of others? (PNc 5)
Or rather, let there be joking with others; for on this earth there is no other king equal to Your Majesty.
When his vision, which has cast aside all policy, falls upon them, even the sky-dwellers flee; what then of others?
O playful one, this exchange you have made between these two necklaces—who, O Lord, would not find words to describe it, were their heart not crooked? (5.74)
"O King, this necklace was not placed upon the chest of the daughter of the serpent-king by you;
rather, this string was fashioned for yourself by the Mind-born God (Kāma) as a means to achieve some desired end of his own."
"Indeed, I shall divert your mind with this necklace of Śaśiprabhā;
and she too, O fair-limbed one, shall become sufficiently moistened by the essence of affection for you, her heart being full."
It is fitting for you to approach the daughter of the king of serpents out of regard for your own arrows;
let your arrow be directed elsewhere. Does that which is subject to your request not grant it? Indeed, it must.
Leave the banks of this lake; take to the path along the sandy shore of the Revā. Quell the glances of the female serpents, who harbor an affection for the form of the Lord of Serpents.
Having heard those charming words of hers—"I am going for the sake of seeing Śaśiprabhā"—that king spoke to her, whose eyes were as pure as a serpent's:
"O auspicious lady, I have already given my word that I shall remain here; your command is not to be transgressed."
Then that girl, speaking deviously, moved forward with the protector of the earth before her;
and the king, his robust wonder shimmering, felt it in his heart as follows: *PNc_5.80*

Then he, whose gait was playful like that of a rutting elephant and who was naturally lovely, made the pretext of requesting golden arrows;

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Departure for the Purpose of Beholding Śaśiprabhā," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita*, composed by Padmagupta— also known by the name Parimala— the son of the illustrious Mṛgāṅkagupta. **The Sixth Canto**
Then, even that daughter of the lord of serpents conceived a longing for that ornament of kings, whose name was indicated by the mark of Bāṇa, as she described her own condition.
Suddenly, the god of love placed his foot upon her heart,
like a passionate bee alighting on a cluster of aśoka blossoms.
It was a marvel that she became subject to the lord of the earth even by name;
for there is no weapon here that the god of love does not possess when he is prepared for battle.
The Malaya breeze, the minister to the empire of the Fish-bannered God, fanned the spark of love within that fawn-eyed woman.
She shone with her fresh youth,
which was playful with the sixty-four arts of love, like a *mālatī* bud with its opening streaks of honey.
With her lotus-like face blooming, its sprout-like lower lip pale-red from being touched by the gentle breath of her sighs, she bore it like a female lotus plant bearing a blossoming lotus.
Upon him, who was so exceedingly simple-hearted, she repeatedly cast her tremulous glances;
she did not cast them upon her circle of friends, as if he were an arrow of that moon among kings.
That letter bearing the name of the king delighted her,
just as the radiance of the rising crescent moon delights the night-lotus.
When that arrow, marked with golden feathers, reached his hand,
that young woman was forcibly made to enter into the initiatory rite of marriage, as it were.
By that bird, whose touch with its copper-red claws had been obtained,
the sprouts were as if released under the pretext of a mass of shimmering luster.
This is the arrow of Sindhurāja, who possesses the form of Kāmadeva, the new Sahasāṅka, and the sole moon of Mālava.
Again and again she recited the name of the King, which was marked by its sweetness, while the moonlight of her teeth played upon her lovely bimba-like lips.
[SYNTAX: *sandānitaka*] Then, having studied with curiosity and having performed the fifth *mūrcchanā*,
the daughters of Pātāla sang before him a song marked with the king’s name.
Even though the king was not yet seen, she became eager for him because of his song;
for the fifth note was the foremost fuel for the fire of the bodiless god of love upon awakening.
She trembled, adorned with blossoming flowers of graceful charm,
like a forest creeper under the touch of the wind of the god of love.
With her body kissing the marks of his passion clearly revealed,
she announced her new love to her clever friends even without a word.
Then Śaśiprabhā, with her face like the autumn moon, spoke thus to her circle of friends with words drenched by the flowing nectar of ambrosia, yet with an air of feigned reserve.
"O friends, who is this King of Sindhu, who has been brought to non-difference from the moon, made a companion by the banner of the peacock, and is being scrutinized by Sahasrāṅka?"
"Why do you remain thus silent? Break your silence and speak!
For within me there now forcibly blossoms a sprout of curiosity."
Then her friend, the perfected maiden named Mālyavatī, spoke to her with words moistened by the nectar of a smile: "Mālyavatī. (PNc 6.20)
"Friend, this king, the ornament of Avanti, is truly audacious;
his fame, white as a *ketaka* flower, is sung even in the city of the serpents."
Once, on the occasion of the festival of the illustrious Mahākāla, I went to the city of Ujjayinī and beheld that thousand-eyed son of Kāśyapa.
O slender lady, that city was graced by him as the sky is by the sun, as the night is by the moon, and as Amarāvatī is by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
It is true that by you alone was Rambhā made to abandon her pride in her beauty; likewise, Nalakūbara was made to do so by the god of love on earth.
When that one of stainless form, who possesses the sixty-four arts,
challenges him to a contest of weight on the scales, what is the sixteen-rayed moon compared to him?
Where indeed do those various innate qualities of that lamp of the earth not shine forth, like the rays of the sun?
Neither among the *nāgas*, nor the *siddhas*, nor among men, nor even among the gods,

Then that daughter of the Siddhas drew his portrait upon the surface of the rock; meanwhile,
the god of love dwelt in the heart of the daughter of the king of horses.
Then she considered that stone slab— which depicted kings and granted all desires merely by being thought of— to be superior even to the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
Then, as he appeared in the painting, the lineages of eyes of the serpent maidens, languid with passion, fell upon the protector of the earth all at once.
Śaśiprabhā also drank him in for a long time with her gaze,
whose lashes were upturned and which made the night-blooming lotuses of her ears appear redundant by its own constant vigilance.
She relished the beauty of that form depicted in the painting,
like a female bee savoring the nectar that accompanies the ambrosia of a lotus.
That slender-waisted woman was brought to a state of agitation by the third [element]:
by an exceedingly intense wonder, and by both intoxication and passion.
That king, though depicted in a painting, entered her heart like the reflection of the moon in the water of a river serene in autumn.
The emergence of her horripilation pierced the vine-like leaf-pattern upon her breast;
for it is true that the external is cast aside by the internal.
Upon her pair of breasts, her sighing caused a slight trembling,
like the evening breeze upon a pair of ruddy geese.
Under the guise of the rows of droplets of perspiration from the beauty of her face,
it was as if a handful of parched grain were scattered for the Love-god as he entered within.
I suspect that the God of Love was seen by her as he straightened his arrow,
for she trembled while her girdle and tiny bells jingled softly.
Addressed by her friend with the words, "He has been seen by you," she, overwhelmed by agitation,
gave a reply with difficulty, in indistinct syllables and with a faltering voice.
Even while the king was painted in a picture, she, through the penetration of his true essence into her mind,
involuntarily turned her moon-like face half-averted with bashfulness.
Seen by her friends with meaningful glances, she cast a bashful smile upon the sprout of her young lower lip, like a *mādhavī* creeper bearing a flower.
"New love, new longing, and those various new desires"—
in this way, her inner circle remained exactly as it was.
With a smile, uncaused and tinged with a touch of bashfulness, possessing the luster of a lotus petal, she seemed to honor that moon-like king.
And she, pressed against the king’s chest as he lay upon her arm,
suddenly succumbed to lassitude, writhing and twisting her limbs.
At that very moment, it was a marvel that the slender maiden became absorbed in him;
whom does this rogue, whose weapon is the flower, not deceive?
Restrained by her vow, that woman with long, fawn-like eyes stood as if insentient, as if empty, as if asleep, and as if painted in a picture.
The slender-waisted woman was pierced in some vital spot by the God of Love,
for even while she was not asleep, her eyes remained closed for a moment like buds.

By means of that new passion, which was a kinsman to the erotic sentiment and possessed the playful gestures of the bodiless god of love, the slender maiden became as if fashioned into someone entirely different.
Because she looked straightforwardly at whatever was wonderful and whatever was shy,
she was perceived by her friends— even though her inner feelings were deeply concealed— by that very act.
Then a friend named Anaṅgavatī spoke thus to her,
as if sprinkling the forest with nectar by means of the moonlight of her teeth.
O you who are like a digit of the moon in the underworld, will this moon of the middle world bring joy to your eyes, which are like white water-lilies?
By this [wind], which is graced by the filaments of lotuses awakened by the forest breeze,
a thrill of horripilation, as it were, has been borne from the sight of you.
Today our eyes have become fruitful, since we have beheld in this painting this moon of Avanti, whose beauty surpasses that of Kandarpa himself.
I think you too were deceived, since these two eyes of yours have been cast with playful grace upon his chest like two strings of pearls.
"He has conquered; he is someone extraordinary. Truly, Kāma is his servant, since your agitation reaches its highest pitch on his account."
O moon-faced one, why do you feel shame here as if you were bound by affection? Who can transgress the irresistible whims of Love?
O friend, who else is more cruel than the god of love,
by whom an arrow has been discharged even at your delicate limbs?
"O slender one, that passion was previously seen only on your lips;
now, O fawn-eyed one, it is observed even in your heart."
O slender-waisted one, the necklace was carried away by one royal swan;
but by this second one, though he is merely a painting, you have captivated the heart.
Why do you feel shame before these women when you slightly lift your face? Oh, how great is your excessive curiosity for this!
This restless blue lotus on her ear, positioned near the corner of her eye,
seems to tell you news of yourself through the humming of its bees.
"Aha! Though situated at a great distance, you are touched in your heart by the moon-like king;
like a moonstone, you are permeated with moisture."
The more you sigh so deeply and subtly, O clever one,
the more clearly this passion of yours begins to breathe.
O lady of restless eyes, this smile of yours, mingled with bashfulness,
is the glory arising from youth that has conquered childhood.
"O fair-limbed one, from the way you feel this distress and the way you tremble,
I fearlessly suspect that Madana has taken up his armor against you."
"What can I do here? This [garland] of yours is firmly bound until the end of time, and this mango blossom has emerged as a weapon of the God of Love."

"Why do you languish? I shall bring him to your side this very moment"—thus does this sweet-voiced cuckoo seem to console you.

Or perhaps some of these brave warriors will themselves become his own people here this very moment by the power of fate,
just as in the forest the monkeys Hanumān, Aṅgada, the son of Pataṅga, and others became the subjects of the Lord of the Raghus.

Since you were addressed by the beloved of Purukutsa regarding the sight of Vaṅku and Muni, it occurs to me that there was some sign from you; for how could you, who are an expert in interpreting facial expressions, have failed to perceive her gesture?

I observe the omen, and from it I know this: before long, within the assembly hall, you will place a golden lotus as an ear-ornament upon the hand of that lady with the long-lashed eyes, a hand whose hair stands on end with thrill.
O Lord, stay right here in this abode of jewels, for indeed there is no such need;
having slain the Asura, I shall bring back that golden lotus instantly at that very moment.
O Lord of Men, that I am victorious over those who conquer the senses is due to the power of the dust of your feet;
that the dawn dispels the blinding darkness is due to the radiance of the sun’s rays. (PNc 10.40)
When Ramāṅgada had ceased after speaking these words— the sequence of which was a progression of political prowess blossoming with tender expressions—

Whose speech could this eloquence be, which, from a mouth other than yours, shines forth with the expansion of doubt utterly dispelled?
From the moon, what cluster of light could emerge that pierces the darkness of even the most wretched night?
I know your prowess; without you, I am not able to maintain my body anywhere.
For my mind is steeped in firm affection for you, just as a bow is infused with the scent of a strong attachment to its long string.
"Come, let us both proceed together quickly toward the city of the Lord of the Three Worlds;
for procrastination, which is incompatible with talk of undertaking a task, does not lead to success in a causeless endeavor."
Having addressed his attendant with these words of the parrot, that ornament of the Malwa deer became silent;

Then, as the parrot uttered the words of the hero so beautifully, the king experienced a wonder beyond even wonder;

O lady of curved limbs, when you had not yet come within the range of my vision even though the darkness of the clouds had vanished,

O deer-eyed one with long eyes, though my heart was already won by you, I did not come to the city of the enjoyers; for I was suddenly carried away by the news of the golden lotus, which was like a river flowing from the birth of the moon [your fame].

I remember your face— the moonlight for the world of serpents— with its lower lip exceedingly pale red, slightly bent down by modesty, radiant with the beauty of a smile, adorned with steady jeweled earrings, and its lotus-eyes closed by the knitting of those outer corners.

I suddenly beheld your footprints upon a path strewn with golden sand.

"What does she paint with her mind? What does she do now? And what does that moon-faced woman say?"—alas, my heart is as if pierced by a thorn because of these thoughts set in motion by you, who have questioned me thus.

O lotus-eyed one, this necklace of yours, beautiful as the mass of rays from the autumn moon, sprinkles me, as it were, upon my heart with its cool spray of light that rises incessantly amidst its intense heat.

Tell me, my beloved: does even that string of pearls upon your two breasts—which, like a friend, has its cool and radiant rays applied as a thick paste of sandalwood—fail to alleviate your fever of love?
O girl of pure smiles, alas, for even a moment you have fallen from the path of my memory while I was longing for you;
O lotus-faced one, did the flower-arrowed god suddenly enter my heart and paint you there?
With her lotus-hand, whose bracelet was darkened by the mass of falling collyrium-stained tears,
she supported the moon-like orb of her face, its pale and emaciated cheeks.
Seated upon a throne that was the playful coral carpet of the King of Love, her sides were adorned with ever-fresh lotus petals, lotus stalks, and garlands.
With the warm breath of her sighs, she was casting the luster of her lip into disrepute— a lip as rosy as a young sprout and a *kaustubha* jewel from the ocean of beauty.

O daughter of the serpent king, I shall constantly behold you with trepidation, for you do not even remember yourself due to the agitation caused by the vast web of my numerous thoughts and mental constructions.
O lotus-eyed one, close your eyes for a brief moment and let us speak; O young woman, know that I have come here having swiftly carried off that golden lotus from the enemy of the gods. (PNc 10.69)
"Noble one, go; let my words, moistened by the intense affection of Ratnacūḍa, become an ear-ornament for that fawn-eyed woman.
Alas, at the end of the curse, O brother, you shall surely forget it; therefore, taking some token from her yourself, you must come back to my side with her reply."

Having thus set a snare for the deer of his mind within the king’s heart with these words, which were like water to a thirsty man and swords to others, Śuka suddenly withdrew his gaze from the sky; and that god, marked by daring, was likewise instantly eager to depart.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Dispatch of Ratnacūḍa," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* composed by Padmagupta, also known as Parimala, the son of Śrī Mṛgāṅkadatta.
**Eleventh Canto:
The Departure for Victory over the Enemy**
Then, carrying the slender-waisted woman with a heart still full of passion,
that lord of the earth set forth, holding the vine-like bow in his hand.

he momentarily appeared like Kṛṣṇa, having assumed the dark luster of that gem.

The lotus plant, with the humming bees sporting within the expanse of her lotus-face,

At every step, those women with eyes like those of wild forest does— whose expansive glances were like the radiance of the moon— led him to an indescribable state of moistened tenderness.
They partook of coconut water rivaling ambrosia,
and tasted betel leaves, cardamom, areca nuts, and betel-vine leaves.
He made beds of the young shoots of golden plantain trees with their bodies spread out,
and he made seats of the broad surfaces of moonstone slabs.
Their singular delight was withdrawn from the duties appropriate to that time,
as they listened to the story of the daughter of the King of Serpents, which was dear to them and had been recounted during their return journey.
With camphor, lotus stalks, and lotus petals placed upon their hearts,
they suffered the fever of love stirred up by the warbling of flocks of male cuckoos.
On his way, he made several halts there, forming friendships with those who had found refuge in groves of *jāmbūnada* creepers.

then Ramangada spoke to that lord of the middle world.

Therefore, at this moment, the daughters of the sages gaze upon you with eyes wide with curiosity, as if looking at the full-orbed moon.

I suspect that Kandarpa, having discharged his arrows among women, has now abandoned his bow and, as if out of remorse for his actions toward the gods, practices asceticism while wielding a staff.

Wearing matted locks, tawny like the clouds of twilight, hanging down from his shoulders,

Without having answered your question, I cannot endure to remain,

He who became the staff for the blue parasol of the sky, which stood above the universe like a shaft of sunbeams.

Pale with autumnal clouds above and dark with groves of *tālī* trees below,

He who set in motion the extensive succession of the seven sacrificial threads and rendered the waters of the ocean the only remnant of the ancient tortoise.

He who brought about the initiation of widowhood for the Hūṇa women by depriving them of their bracelets, armlets, anklets, and girdles.

Surely those who possess such unfeigned generosity were fashioned by the Creator from the very atoms used to create wish-fulfilling jewels.

"Before long, Śaśiprabhā shall become your bride here,

"Be steadfast; having stayed in this forest of asceticism for a measured time, let the fatigue born of the long journey be dispelled by you."

**The Twelfth Canto** Then, she [the goddess] approached him, who bore the mark of the fish of Manu and was seated upon a jeweled couch.
The daughter of the king of serpents fell upon the path of his memory, she who is the sole ornament of the world.
He directed his affection toward those objects before his eyes which were most desirable;
yet, by means of hundreds of rising longings, he made them instead the very seat of his discontent.
By the frequent twisting of her creeper-like limbs, by her sighs, and by her vacant glances,
the King’s state of being possessed by the trappings of love was inferred by those standing near him.
Then Ramāṅgada became diligent in attending to him during the cool season, fanning him with the breeze from plantain leaves and placing lotus stalks and bulbs upon his heart.
For the king, who was tormented by love, there were only two things that served as diversions for his mind:
the beautiful-eyed woman becoming a guest in his hands, and that arrow marked with sandalwood paste from her breasts.
Though separated from Madana, he was overcome on the path by the fatigue that had arisen;
for a moment he stood motionless, his face obscured by the moonlight-white linen cloth.
Then, his sprout-like feet being gently massaged with reverence by his attendant,
he was quickly kissed upon the eyes by sleep, as if by a fawn-eyed woman.
Then the king, longing for his beautiful-faced beloved in the grove outside his own city because of her appearance in his dream, gazed upon her as she sat upon his lap, adorned with golden lotuses.
She was lovely as she cast her sidelong glance with an eye that surpassed the petals of a blue lotus,
while her face— with its pale cheeks— was turned away in modesty.

With her hand, whose pearl bracelets had slipped loose, she repeatedly and imperceptibly pushed aside the breast-cloth— pure as the rays of the autumn moon— which was falling away due to her trembling.

Bearing upon her lower lip— a beauty like a fresh sprout, as if the God of Love had recently taken up residence there— the shimmering mass of rays from her moon-like face, which was a flash of a gentle smile.
Her body, adorned with drops of perspiration during the festival of the world’s sole gaze,
appeared like the Goddess Śrī risen from the ocean after it was struck by Mount Mandara, dripping with clinging nectar.

On her left breast, which was trembling intensely from the embrace of her own hand— its fingers rendered powerless by the throbbing of her passion— the eyes, bristling with horripilation, cast glances of extreme alarm.

She wore earrings of exceedingly radiant jewels and was adorned with a most lovely, long necklace; her golden girdle hung loosely upon her hips, like the presiding deity of the god of unequalled arrows.
[SYNTAX: A Kulaka] Then, with a smile and trembling seized, she fell upon the path of the arrows of the God of Love; these words were spoken by the Hero:
Thus, with words moistened by affection, he indeed spoke to that lotus-faced woman.
This face of yours, beautiful with its braided hair, does not shine from behind;
O lady, it is as if the orb of the moon were embraced by a streak of dark clouds.
O lady of graceful limbs, this face of yours, as if obstructed by the jewel on your armlet and driven back by shame, is unable to turn toward me; what recourse is there?
O fair-limbed one, this side-long glance of yours— half-cast toward your lower lip, with eyes rippling with sweet sidelong glances,
and darkened at the corners— is white in the middle and bestows great beauty.

O fair-toothed one, this breeze— cool at the end of day as it approaches evening— is somehow most desirable to me, for it has mingled with the line of your cheek, its surface moistened by drops of perspiration.
O lotus-eyed one, this blue water-lily, its hue as pale-red as your bimba-fruit lips, gazes upon you;
behold, for the sun now desires to set his foot upon the crest of the western mountain.

O Lakṣmī of Love, as you were being carried away through the sky by this Kṛṣṇa, your two eyes were stolen by him who bears the Sudarśana discus— the destroyer of misfortune— which is the very image of the Sun-god with his thigh-born charioteer.
The red morning garment of the lotus-creeper, held by the hand that is the sun-lotus,
is now being drawn toward the maiden of the western quarter by the sun, who has turned his face away.
O proud lady, this pair of cakravāka birds— with eyes fixed on one another in compassion, and with lotus-fiber shoots falling away as they gradually separate— seems to moisten my very heart.
Look, O timid one; now a triad is being separated from its triad:
the sun from its radiance, the lotus from its beauty, and this bird from its mate, who is shedding tears.
From the belly of the pond that is the sky, the sun-lotus— possessing a deep crimson luster and filaments of rays as smooth as gold— is cast away by Time, who acts like an elephant with dark tusks.
As the sun, carried away by passion, kisses the western quarter before him,
this slender-waisted lady of the east becomes dark-faced, marked as it were by the wrath of Indra.

Behold, here the forest lands shine with clusters of exceedingly red sunlight; they appear like the splendor of Day marked by the footprints of Night, dyed with lac, as she celebrates her union with the Sun.
O lady with intoxicating eyes, look ahead toward the western quarter:
the sun, agitated by his heavy stumbling over [your] name, enters a motionless course.
O beautiful one, whatever was suddenly abandoned by this friend of the lotuses was simultaneously gazed upon from here by the darknesses stationed at the mouths of mountain caves.
O lady with lips like young shoots, the sun, a traveler on the path of the celestial highway, has ceased his journey;
he now rests upon the surface of the sunset mountain, its rocky floor smoothed by his own rays.
This wife of the sun casts her gaze, unmarked by the ripples of sound, upon the pair— the sun, red as fresh saffron, and her beloved moon, distressed by separation.
"You have departed; tell me where, for I am not able to endure separation from you"—thus the lotus plant, with her hands folded like a lotus bud, seems to entreat her beloved.
O lady of faultless limbs, this orb of the sun, resembling a mirror reddened by molten lac from its accumulated tawny rays, is now sinking away beyond the western mountain.
The sun has departed somewhere in secret along with the splendor of the lotuses;
tell me, O lady of curved limbs, how will the day-lotus pass this night without him?
O fair-toothed one, as the intense glow of twilight spreads forth, the sky has become on one side like a stretch of polished coral, rising up in harmony with the expanse of your sidelong glances.
O friend, whom do these quarters of the sky not captivate at evening with their dense, enchanting, and saffron-colored clouds,
which appear like saffron-ochre from the twilight glow clinging to them?
Indeed, the noble twilight has been violated by the darkness facing the night;
like an angry woman, she quickly turns back, her anklets being the excessively talkative birds.
O fierce one, that lotus, smeared by the twilight glow of your body,
is being mocked by this face with its coppery cheeks, due to the mingling of the luster of your jeweled earrings.
O beautiful one, it is as if the twilight has suddenly departed to announce to the Lord of Day that the darkness has arisen and that lotus, your beloved, has fallen into dejection.
O slender-waisted one, that light deposited in the sacrificial offerings was quickly consumed by the Sun,
as if it were the radiance of the Mind-born God flashing forth from his own arrows upon your bashful glances.

First there was darkness like the flax flower upon your face; then followed the luster of the nipples of your breasts; now, however, a dense darkness, thick as a young tamāla tree, has spread everywhere.

O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, this pleasure garden is closing its eyes: the śārikas are silent in the hollows of the trees, the cuckoos have settled into their own nests, and the peacocks are overcome by sleep.

Now the world is being plunged into darkness by the shadows spreading from the depths of mountain caves, possessing the beauty of garlands of blue lotuses, just as a lotus pond is entered by elephants.
By means of this white lily, which possesses a row of long lashes and is beautiful with streaks like collyrium for dispelling darkness,
the night-lotus attains splendor as if by her very eye.
Out of curiosity for the two bees dwelling within its belly, as it were, to hear their indistinct speech,
the darkness remains hidden and motionless within the joints of the lotus petals.
O you with tremulous eyes of exceedingly bright and dark luster, as your two eyes swing to and fro here,
the darkness intensifies upon your cheeks, which are marked with lines of agaru paste.
O lady with curling locks, this sky, illuminated in an instant by stars risen here and there,
shines as if marked all around by drops of sweat born from the intense heat of the day.
Behold the eastern quarter of Mahendra, variegated by the luster of the moon amidst the darkness,
like the throat of the Lord of Umā, streaked with the radiance of the smile of the Daughter of the Mountain King.
O daughter of the serpent king, behold this first risen digit of the moon;
oh, it shines in the direction of Indra’s quarter like a young woman with a fresh nail-mark.
O long-eyed one, if you have curiosity, before long I shall place this soft, playful bracelet upon your hand, which has the luster of a lotus petal and is moist with nectar.
Is your face, known to be faultless and standing before you, not equal to the moon? For that [moon], out of shame for its spot, does not suddenly ascend into the sky.
Behold, this risen orb of the moon possesses a beauty that makes this very quarter of the sky resemble your face,
with its clear cheeks adorned by distinct streaks of black aloe-paste.
Behold here, upon the face of the Night-bride, as her garment of darkness falls away and her pupils gradually become visible, the white-rayed crescent-earring shines forth.
O lotus-eyed one, the moon surely scrapes away the darkness with its rays;
for behold, upon the night-lotuses, its fragments fall like bees.
This sapphire, struck by the rays of the moon which have obscured its brilliance,
slowly dissolves within the caves of the lord of mountains, shrinking back once more.
Behold: under the guise of her smooth, shimmering orb, this night draws forth from the moon-casket for the sake of the sky this very necklace of pearls.
When the world was thus shrouded in darkness, O lotus-petal-eyed one,
this very world has now been illuminated from afar by the moon, pale as a root of saffron.

O lady of curved limbs, the moonlight appears as if it has spread out within the hollows of your eyes, yet shrinks back at the presence of your forehead mark; it seems to be held captive within your strings of pearls.
Reflected in your two breasts, even this single moon becomes twofold,
like the casket of the nectar-ocean of your loveliness opened by Fate.

O moonlight of the world of serpents, the crescent moons of your face have fallen upon these two cheeks— which have stolen the beauty of the *mugdha-madhūka* flower— almost as if out of a desire for touch.
O moon-faced one, see how this man has become desirable because of you, just as this deer-marked moon has become so because of its union with the night.
O slender-waisted one, the bow is being ascended by the vine of Cupid’s bowstring,
just as a mountain on a sandbank is ascended by the tide of the ocean when it is raised by the moon.
Now, after hundreds of mutual endearments, the bees remain within the lotus-dwellings, which are fragrant with pollen moistened by nectar.

O proud lady, here this pair of royal swans, damp with affection, sleeps while being gently fanned from this side by the wind, which is like a friend to the Maruts and releases the fragrance of white water-lilies.
"O Cakravāka bird, this one before us is cooing piteously, 'Alas, poor thing!
O compassionate one, she is sufficient as a witness here for us; it is therefore proper for you to go from here."
Having thus addressed that woman, the sweet-spoken lord of the earth-dwellers, being well-pleased, entered with her, it is said,
a cave in a great pleasure-mountain.
Then, accompanied by her, that youth sat upon a surface of moonstone, which bore a sweet and auspicious luster arising from the sudden blending of its vivid qualities.

Thereafter, with charming and affectionate words, he brought that fair-faced woman— who had turned her face away in shame and whose full breasts were adorned with horripilation— to a state of compliance.

Then that lord of subjects beheld the face of the fair-eyed woman, its eyes slow with emotion, its smiling mouth bowed with shame, and its cheeks moist with perspiration, all graced by a gentle smile.
That the moon-faced maiden appeared indeed as if she were modest, that she seemed indeed to look straight ahead,
and that she remained as if painted— by that alone, O King, she truly captivated his mind.

Having wiped his face, which was stained with the pollen from the blue lotuses on her ears, the lover removed the decorative mark from the beautiful-eyed woman’s forehead— a mark that had become muddy with the water of her tears.
Then the Lord, captivated by her peerless love, led her— who had cast aside her modesty—
to the mastery of the arts of amorous play, just as a leader of a herd leads a female elephant.

With her mass of hair loose and disheveled, her moist cheeks being rubbed, the luster of the jewel on her lower lip fading, and the orb of her moon-like face easily betraying perspiration; // PNc_12.73 //

With her pearl necklace broken and cast aside, with the cosmetic paste on her body rubbed away by a tight embrace, and with her trembling hand placed upon her breast adorned with incomplete nail-marks; // PNc_12.74 //
Then, with her eyes half-closed in a growing sense of increasing shame,
that daughter of the serpent king attained, it is said, an indescribable state of bliss.

As he skillfully fanned her breasts, which were covered in blossoming beads of perspiration, with the breeze from lotus petals, his fatigue was thereby dispelled by that long-eyed one. (SYNTAX: *kulakam*)
Then, with her garment held fast by modesty, her girdle’s thread slipped down from her hips, and her blue-lotus ear-ornament resting upon her eyes, he led that woman to his own lap.
It is said that Sudṛśa placed the crest-jewel, which had slipped from another, upon his own head;
and with fingers reddened, he reportedly arranged his hair into graceful curls and twists.

"Look here, young woman, this row of letters written upon the surface of the mirror is your face turned back toward me," was heard by Ramāṅgada, whose face was smiling, as his own husband spoke words of love from within a dream.
Then, as the parrot Śuci, perched upon a tree in the courtyard of the hermitage hut, clearly recited the Sāman hymn,
the sleep of the king— who had forcibly brought about a reunion with his beloved— was utterly shattered.
When the union with his beloved, which had appeared in his dream, suddenly vanished, the king once again closed his eyes in hope of her;
for a moment he remained as if painted in a portrait. Alas, how great is the audacity of the god of love, who shatters even the fortitude of such men!

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Dream-Encounter with the Daughter of the Serpent King," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* composed by Padmagupta, also known as Parimala, the son of Śrī Mṛgāṅkadatta.
The thirteenth canto begins:
Then, thus deceived by the prowess of the five-arrowed god [Kāma], he opened his eyes with a yawn.
The king’s earrings were pressed against his shoulders by his arms, which were raised and turned as he clasped her fingers.
As he had clearly experienced in union with the eyes of the fawn-eyed girl while his sleep was overcome by fatigue,
that vision suddenly became indistinct in his heart upon waking, like an ancient painting.
"Surely the cosmetic paste from her breasts must have been transferred to me by her slender-waisted form," he thought;
thus, deluded by passion, he slowly stroked his own body with eyes clouded by sleep.
Removing the ornament from his left ear, Smara likewise overwhelmed him with arrows,
so that his fortitude melted away from his mind like water from a pearl-oyster shell.
Then, fixing his gaze— stilled by dejection— upon him standing nearby,
he sighed in such a way that the garlands of pearl nets from the canopy repeatedly took on a dark, somber hue.
"By what doe-eyed woman have you been made to undergo the labor of painting decorative leaf-designs upon your cheeks?
Thus he spoke to him with a playful jest.
Rāmāṅgada, with his armlet slightly loosened, [spoke].
Then, wearing a smile as white as a pearl and possessing teeth whose luster surpassed the glow of coral,
the lotus-eyed one related to him his encounter with the daughter of the serpent king, which had occurred in a dream.
Then, for that graceful prince, his companion increased his delight with stories as if they were nectar;
consequently, neither the breeze from lotus leaves nor sandalwood paste was sufficient to soothe the fever of love.
His right arm, ever consecrated to the protection of the earth, throbbed violently— not out of haste to seize a golden lotus, but because his inner heart was distressed with anxiety.
Then there was the arrival of the sage Vaṅku, wearing a bright golden bark-garment, with matted locks hanging down from his shoulders,
and his right lotus-hand held up, adorned with a shimmering rosary of crystal beads.

The lord of the people beheld the great sage Vaṅku approaching with his disciples near the women’s quarters, followed by deer who were always fondled with tips of *darbha* grass and adorned with ornaments for their large eyes.
Releasing his cross-legged posture and looking out from the jeweled palace with haste,
he immediately performed a respectful prostration before him, whose ground was illuminated by the radiance of the gems in his crown.
Then, having received his blessing, the sage sat down upon a deer skin spread over a jeweled altar;
and by his permission, those moons among kings took their seats upon the moonstone slabs.

"O Great King, has this body of yours been abandoned through the exhaustion born of traveling the long road? Having thus received the guest-offering with great joy, the sage then asked the crest-jewel of kings: *munipraśnaḥ api śrameṇāyatamārgajanmanā tanur mahārāja taveyam ujjhitā / muniḥ praharṣeṇa kṛtārhaṇas tadā sa rājacūḍāmaṇim ity apṛcchata //* 13.14 *//* [The sage’s question: "O Great King, has this body of yours been cast aside due to the fatigue arising from the long journey? Having been honored with great delight, the sage then questioned that crest-jewel of kings in this manner."
Then,
as if covering his face with the hem of his garment white as frost by means of the rays of his teeth,
that king, receiving the words of the monarch, began to speak these words, charming with their natural courtesy.
"O father, these particles of dust from your feet, clinging to my prostrations, dispel my fatigue;
for how long can the exhaustion of day linger upon the night-lily, which is kissed by the rays of the moon?"

While their mutual conversation concerning the sight of the monkey was still unfolding, as the sage rested in the depths of the human world and the underworld, the king’s mind became eager for his saddle; just then, he desired to question him.
By this [monkey], first of all, was seen standing before him the long-tailed Valīmukha,
as bright as snow, like the foot of the Lord of Ambikā from which the daughter of Jahnu has emerged upon the ground below.
Holding in his hand a pomegranate, as red-hued as the cheek of a honey-intoxicated Kerala woman,
he resembled the son of Anjana in his childhood, who had drawn out the orb of the sun at dawn in hopes of seizing its fruit.
[SYNTAX: *sandānitaka*] Indeed, the monkey was like the bestower of the fruit for those two—Dharma and Kāma—which are desired by the three worlds; such was the meaning of those two.
Standing between the Moon of the Lord of Sages and the Earth-Moon, he was beheld by the ascetics with smiling faces.
Then, filled with wonder, that Indra of the middle world accepted the fruit offered by him—
just as the subduer of the Ten-Necked One had accepted the crest-jewel of Maithilī, which was as red as a hibiscus flower, from the son of the Wind-god.

He shone intensely with that very self of his— which was the abode of innate splendor, impassioned, adorned by hands marked with the signs of royalty, and naturally possessing perfect conduct— just as he did before.
Repeatedly observing the deep redness of her unripened fruit, which was intensified by the fresh heat of the sun,
he remembered the bimba-like lip of the fawn-eyed girl— resembling a young sprout— and fell into a state of desolation.
