Then, from his hand—which was slipping from the wristband and whose fingers were trembling with a shudder—that [ring] fell upon the golden floor as if it were lagging behind; it shattered instantly like a pomegranate fruit.
Then, from within that [palace], there emerged a shimmering mass of jewels, stealing the splendor of the *kiṃśuka* flower,
like a shower of sparks from the eye of the Three-eyed God (Śiva) out of anger toward the flower-bowed god (Kāmadeva).

Then, by means of these two— the forest-dweller of disciplined conduct and the ruby-like pomegranate with its scattered luster— the king, the subduer of the earth, was led to the very pinnacle of wonder.
And Śakra, gratified by that wonderful gift, placed upon the monkey’s hand the jeweled bracelet from the Revā river,
just as Hari places his weapon upon a fragment of cloud white as the moon at the end of the rainy season.

Then, in an instant, the king no longer beheld that man before him as Hari, but rather as one who had cast off his form like the moon, appearing instead with a body dark as fresh collyrium and adorned with various ornaments.
Having prostrated before the sage, his mind filled with wonder, he cast a respectful glance at Ramāṅgada;
then, with palms joined in reverence and golden earrings swaying upon his cheeks, he offered his salutation to the king.
The question posed by the sage was adorned; "Whose lineage are you descended from? Where is your station? And what monkey were you?
To him, the sage replied with a look full of wonder and waves of emotion, having been gazed upon by the king with an intent look.
Then he spoke the words of Śaśikhaṇḍa, pleasing the quarters with the rays of his teeth, which were like the beams of the charming moon.
He spoke these words, as steady as the deep resonance of a row of clouds heavy with the weight of fresh rain.
"O Lord of Sages, I am Śaśikhaṇḍa, the son of Śikhaṇḍaketu, the ruler of the Vidyādharas;
my residence is on the Moonstone Mountain, whose jeweled neck is frequented by celestial maidens."
"It is said that an image of the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu), made of great sapphire, emerged from the ocean itself";
having heard this report, the women of the city went from here to Maṇidvīpa to behold it.
"I too have a great curiosity regarding her; therefore come, let us go, for I join my palms in supplication to you.
Perhaps at some point, having approached me suddenly, my beloved Mālatī entreated me thus while prostrating herself.
Then, as he flew swiftly through the sky, which was blue as a blue lotus, together with her on one side,
O father, that ocean— capable of bearing the weight of the king of mountains— suddenly fell within the range of my vision.
With its waves rising upward like hands laden with heaps of various jewels and pearls,
the ocean seemed intent on offering a priceless guest-offering to the Sun, the single eye of the world.
With its interior as rosy as the luster of fresh coral, his hand was marked by the *śārṅga* bow like that of Murāri;
he was adorned by the daughter of the great seer Jahnu, like the broad mass of matted hair of the enemy of Andhaka.

The waters, turbid with the ichor of the elephants of the quarters submerged within them, blocked all directions with the roars of new clouds— roars that distressed the sea-monsters and plunged deep into the bottomless depths of the netherworld.
Its splendor was enhanced on all sides by the clusters of rays from shimmering jewels rising from its base,
resembling the bows of the Lord of Puloma’s Daughter set against the backdrop of hundreds of clouds appearing at the end of an eon.
It was rendered wondrous by the large-eyed *timi* fish, who— mistaking the circles of clouds resting near the shore for islands long since vanished—
gazed upon them with wide eyes as they began playful frolicking like aquatic elephants.
On that path, he encountered women whose breasts were firm and well-formed, inspiring longing in those like him;
in some places, he saw shells upon the rocks as beautiful as the autumn moon, appearing like water-nymphs.

In some places, the sky was scraped by great mountains whose peaks were marked by their own torrents and whose mud was streaked with them; mountains where heaps of jewels were gathered in vast caves, and from which tortoises had been pulled out after they had sunk deep below.
In some places, bearing newly sprouted coral shoots tossed by the winds of the surging tide,
they appeared like upward-reaching crests of the submarine fire, red as the rising sun.
In some places, a cloud dark as a blade of *dūrvā* grass, resting upon a mass of foam white as nectar,
clearly seemed to have been granted lordship by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow reclining upon the couch of the king of serpents above.
In some places, the rocks on the banks possess the luster of the interiors of white water-lilies; in others, they are as dark as deep blue lotuses;
and in yet others, they are as pale-red as a parrot’s beak, their surfaces variegated with pearls.
In that very same way, as I was traveling along a path dark as the *tāla* tree, which was like a mass of clouds,
the crest-jewel of the fawn-eyed woman fell down, its setting loosened and its binding undone by my haste.
As I was running along, the rays [of the sun], whose sprout-like shoots were being torn away by my fingernails at intervals,
entered the interior of the ocean, appearing like a radiant *kośāmra* tree reddened by its clusters of blossoms.
But as he was turning back, forcibly dragged by the hand of the horse that blocked the sky,
the roaring ocean, like an elephant, in an instant cast him away somewhere into the depths of the underworld.

Then, while wandering there, I beheld with wonder a woman carrying in her hand a brilliantly shining jewel; she appeared like the embodied form of Smara’s pride, or like my own personification, as she entered the ascetic grove.
Therefore, since you did not return the crest-jewel of my beloved even though I requested it again and again,
I have now forcibly seized her two jeweled sandals marked with crocodiles, which belong to the God of Love.
"Why is this hermitage empty of those whose wealth is asceticism? Alas! By this thief I have been robbed!
Thus she wailed piteously, speaking repeatedly with words faltering from the rising of tears.
Then, upon hearing that sound of weeping, a certain sage of great asceticism emerged in haste from his crystal stone palace,
like the sun, radiant as the *tamāla* tree, emerging from a cloud.
"Father, this ornament of mine has been forcibly taken from your hermitage by someone," he said;
at these words, he took up his anger as fire takes up its flame through the pouring of oblations.

With his terrible brow knit together, gazing with an eye whose fierce pupils were tawny like a meteor, and his lower lip quivering with intense rage, he spoke these words, rejecting the prostrations of the one who had bowed before him: *śāpavarṇanam* (The Description of the Curse) *PNc_13.54*
In this penance grove, even the flowers of the creepers are never plucked by this wind;
yet now, O you who are the ornament of the weak, you have stretched out your hand for the destruction of this rogue soul.
"Since you have committed such an act of treachery against me, become a monkey this very instant!
Then, taking water from his water-pot, he who was like a forest fire cursed me thus.
Then his anger gradually subsided in his mind; for compassion inclines toward one who has repented. A drop of water does not remain long in the hollow of a lotus leaf trembling with ripples.
"O Blessed One, may this remorse of mine be released; such was my destiny.
Therefore, please tell me: when will this darkness, arisen from the mouth of the night of the curse, come to an end?"

When he had been addressed by me in this way, he then spoke thus: "O child, when that son of King Sīyaka comes here from before the sage Vaṅku, he shall place the bracelet from the Narmadā upon your hand."
Ever since he dwelt for a thousand years in the subterranean realm (rasātala) in the form of a monkey,
this moon among kings has now dispelled the darkness of the curse from your hermitage.
O Lord of Sages, whatever has been done by this [man] out of a desire to offer a return favor was done merely as a play; I am not capable of making a return for that.
Can the sun ever be within the scope of a reciprocal service for the moon, whose thinness was licked away by its rays?
Nevertheless, O King, this man should be employed for some minor purpose of your own;
did not the noble Sun, that jewel-lamp of the earth’s surface, command Anūru to perform the task of a charioteer?
Thus addressed by him who was intent on affection, the king’s face became bowed with shame;
for the praises of those who are not such as he are by their very nature prone to kindle pride.
By that praiseworthy narration of his own life, which was as enchanting as the abundance of nectar's essence through its union with the crescent moon,
that lord of the earth instantly attained an indescribable splendor, like the matted locks of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva) joined with Umā.
Then, questioned by him as if he were ignorant of the reason for his arrival upon the surface of the earth,
that protector of the world of men, his bimba-like lips bathed in the nectar of a smile, related his own adventure to him who had heard his pleasant words.
Thereupon, although dispatched by the king, that Vidyādhara did not turn his face toward returning to his own abode;
for those of noble mind feel a certain shame when departing without having rendered even the slightest service to a person who has previously helped them.
"O King, be gracious; let the assembly be convened now, for this servant shall be the one to walk at the forefront of the dust of your feet.
When the great seer had spoken these sweet words, the sovereign finally, with great difficulty, consented.
Then, preceded by the deep resonance of conchs and drums signaling the arrival of the Vidyādhara army, his own host appeared before him in an instant; merely upon being remembered,
it became shrouded in the darkness of the underworld by the mass of rays from the polished blades of their sword-leaves.
Then, having mounted the soaring chariot prepared by him, the lord of men, his hand equipped with a bow,
set out smoothly toward Vajrāṅkuśa, following the auspicious rites for departure as directed by the sage Vaṅku.

As he stood at that moment not far from the door of the hermitage hut, the king was seen for a brief instant by the deer-eyed women who were gazing at him simultaneously; with the mass of rays from their eyes, he appeared as if wearing the pure skin of a deer, consecrated for the ritual of the grand horse sacrifice.

Due to the tumultuous clamor of the army on all sides, that forest of the sage— where the concentration of birds was disturbed, where the young deer were terrified, where the tall reeds were filled with silent parrots, where the peacocks had flown up, and where pairs of deer had ceased their mutual scratching— was thrown into agitation.
Then, on the road, that King Navasāhasāṅka— saluted by the Vidyādharas, with handfuls of wild rice and parched grain offered joyfully by the daughters of the sages,
accompanied by Ramāṅgada, and filling the quarters with the long echoes from the caves of the family mountain caused by the surging waves of musical instruments— ascended toward glory.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Assembly of the Vidyādhara Lords," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* composed by Padmagupta, also known as Parimala, the son of Śrī Mṛgāṅkadatta.
The Fourteenth Canto:
The Ascent into the Sky.
Then, leaving behind the ground at the edge of the hermitage where peacocks were eager for the sound of its wheels,
his chariot ascended to the abode of the Lord of Chariot-Wheels (Viṣṇu) through the power of the Vidyādhara mantras.
The sound of auspicious musical instruments rose before him, thickened by the blast of conchs, heard with trembling by the elephants of the quarters who pricked up their ears in agitation.
The daughters of the ascetics watched him as he traveled through the expanse of the sky with his faces raised upward,
their lovely eyes stretched wide to the ears through the gaps between the leaves of the trees of the hermitage.
Moving in the midst of the hosts of Vidyādharas, that protector of the middle world shone like the moon— the sole source of the nectar of no small beauty— amidst the succession of constellations.

In that place, the eyes of the full-hipped women were not withdrawn; their lashes fluttered with curiosity, and they possessed the grace of blue lotuses drawn toward their ears as they darted glances from the corners of their eyes.

Then, as he stood nearby, Ramāṅgada spoke thus to the Lord of Avanti, who was observing by the thousands the hosts of Vidyādharas moving through the sky before him: “Behold the forces of the Vidyādharas moving through the air by the thousands.”
O King, these Vidyādharas surround your golden chariot, which is adorned with banners, trembling, and marked by a jeweled standard—
just as the Vālakhilyas surround the sun of a thousand rays.
As you walk, with your shoulder-tuft entangled by a garland of *mandāra* flowers dropped by immortal maidens,
and your mass of mane white as a cluster of *kunda* blossoms, you shine like the lion of Kātyāyanī.
Is this sound of yours the roar of the marching trumpets, thickened by its echo within the belly of Pātāla?
Or is it this terrifying clamor of clouds at an untimely end of the aeon spreading forth?
Look! At the base of the earth, this darkness, resembling the soot of collyrium, is seen settled there;
it has been swallowed by the sprouts of light from the jewels in the crowns of the dense Vidyādharas.
Driving away the darkness on all sides with the jewel-staffs of their neck-chains,
these horses, with chowries fanned by the wind, seem to scrape the very sky with their hooves.

Smiling together with the daughters of the Vidyādharas, these handfuls of parched grain for your departure— cast with side-long glances from their eyes— fall upon your chariot, stumbling against the banners.
O Lord of Men, behold before you these sword-blades of the foremost Vidyādharas;
by their dark hue like black collyrium, they assume the appearance of waves upon the great ocean of the sky.
Making the faces of the quarters resonant with the sound of golden bells,
these rows of celestial chariots proceed with great difficulty, their progress obstructed by one another.
This wind,
which causes the flagstaffs of beaten gold to tremble, makes the fluttering silken cloths of the banners— resembling the tender sprouts of *aśoka* clusters and crimson in hue— dance about.
As these sky-dwellers travel along, the mass of saffron dust raised by the mutual friction of their broad shoulders turns the faces of the quarters yellowish-brown.
The sky, its interior filled with the hips of the dark-eyed women— which serve as playful thrones for King Love, adorned with jeweled girdles and bracelets— reaches its end here.
We see these nets of pearls released from the celestial chariots falling from the sky, shimmering through their mutual friction and resembling the rays of the moon, the beloved of the night-lotuses.
As they depart ahead in their celestial chariots, these young women turn back their lotus-faces;
O Lord, with eyes like cupped hands, their tremulous pupils resting upon the outer corners, they drink you in.
From these Vidyādhara women moving swiftly back and forth from here, the jeweled earrings strike against the dark aloe-wood leaf-patterns on their cheeks.
As these celestial chariots collide with one another here from their swift descent,
the pearl necklaces of these women shatter, their central gems swinging to and fro.
These rays from the jeweled earrings of the women, scattered by the agitation of their movement,
fall upon the crest-jewels of the serpents crawling here on the ground and resound there.
Thinking that this netherworld was empty of the moon— the festival for the eyes—
the women here have created, under the guise of their own faces, a creation consisting of moons within the sky.
On one side, the creeper-like swords of the Vidyādharas cause the hero to blossom with passion;
on the other, the glances of the women, long as garlands of fresh blue lotuses, cause the sentiment of love to blossom.
Beholding this army suddenly reflected in the crystal courtyards, it was as if they had seen their own image.
Filled with wonder, the women of Nāgapura cast the lotuses of their eyes toward him from here.

Therefore, O Lord of Men, we have set out from the place of Vaṅku Muni, whose boundary is fragrant with the smoke of sacrificial offerings, because the rows of ascetics there are so preoccupied with beholding you as you traverse the sky.
The description of the forest is as follows:

"This wind approaches before us, drawing along the fragrance of various kinds of flowers; thus I suspect that the forest, with its sky-scraping trees, will soon come within the range of our vision. (PNc 14.27)
O protector of the earth, with these foremost jewels of celestial chariots clearing the path in haste,
this chariot of yours, its banner motionless, proceeds through the sky with great majesty.
Look! This entire range of forest ridges, which was previously hidden from view by the clusters of white blossoms on the trees, has suddenly been revealed in a mere instant. 14.29.
O Lord, since this host of Vidyādharas has descended slightly from the sky,
I perceive that their minds are fixed upon this place out of curiosity to behold the forest.
Behold this army, possessing the dark luster of a row of *tamāla* trees and bearing golden lotuses in the form of Rāma’s face, advancing toward the forest like the daughter of Jahnu toward the ocean.
O Protector of the Earth, this row of celestial chariots standing before you, the king of forest-ranges,
displays the splendor of jeweled crowns, from which the light of gems projects great rainbows.
Behold, these drops of water from the horses' saliva, smeared with blood from wounds inflicted by the bits and bearing the splendor of cochineal insects, roll upon the sprouts of golden trees.
O King, here the creepers, their tips of foliage shaken by the gentle breeze, strive to gather all their flowers as if they were eager to seize the beauty from these women.
These flowers of the trees, with bees nestled within their bellies,
shine like eyes cast upward for the purpose of beholding the graceful charms of the Vidyādharīs.

Look! Having approached this upper window, the jeweled palaces bow forward before the broad-hipped women who are gathering the flowers from the tips of the creepers, as if weighed down by the burden of the king.
As the chains of the brilliance of the jeweled balconies of the great trees cling to the tips of their branches,
this splendor of the jeweled cages seems to be echoed by the celestial chariots as they linger here.

O King, behold these fawn-eyed women standing as if in the sky, engaged in gathering flowers in this forest that is embraced by the splendor of all seasons and filled with birds equal to their own breath.
These graceful women, with hands as fair as golden lotuses,
pluck the tender blossoms from the trees along with their stalks, just as they steal away the hearts of young men.
Behold, above these [trees], the circles of bees rising from the clusters at the tips of the creepers and kissed by the luster of the crest-jewels, give rise to the illusion of blue parasols.
This bee, having smelled the fragrance of the lotus-face of this most beautiful woman, leaves the flowering creeper;
for the minds of those who recognize excellence always delight in superior qualities.

Behold! This creeper, being gracefully bent by this slender-limbed woman as she playfully draws it toward the mango tree, shines like the bow-creeper of Kandarpa, with its rising flowers acting as arrows.
With her gaze flickering toward the swarms of bees circling about, intent on the act of adorning herself with playful ear-ornaments,
she was unable to gather the flowers from the tree that longed for the embrace of her breasts.

Offered by her beloved, this cluster of *aśoka* blossoms— stealing the luster of the lower lip of a woman whose face has been drunk from by her husband— shines with an indescribable brilliance upon her ear-ornament that glows with jewels.

The monkeys, mistaking for pomegranate seeds the pearls that have fallen to the ground from this necklace— strung with intervals by the tossing of her creeper-like arms and stained by the saffron of her breasts— pick them up and scatter them about.

Behold, this flash of laughter from the beauty of the summer heat finds its place upon the hair-braid of her whose face is like a fresh jasmine flower— a braid thick with the fragrance of black aloe-wood incense and dark as a swarm of bees.
O King, having removed from here this ivory ear-ornament, white as a swan’s wing, this young woman places upon her ear a fresh *karṇikāra* flower, which shines with a heated *aṣṭāpada* gem.
This hand of the long-eyed maiden, with fingers as copper-red as young shoots, stands here at the end [of her arm];
from this point, it attains full manifestation through the lines of light from her nails, which shine like the rays of the autumn moon.
As bees fly here and there, lured by the *śirīṣa* flowers on her ears,
this young girl practices a game of ball, as it were, with the restless movements of her glances.
Bearing the smile of the rainy season's charm and a fresh ketaka petal behind her ear,
she shines like a maiden of the Himalayas who has made the crescent moon her beloved ear-ornament.
Once the young monkey had been found by looking at the surface of the cheek in the painting,
the slender woman remained as if painted there in fear, her hand not withdrawing from this *kadamba* tree on the celestial chariot.
Behold, as she gathers *atimuktaka* flowers,
this girl bears her loosened mass of hair upon her shoulder like a dark-blue *tāmāla* palm-leaf fan for the playful sport of Love.
As she casts flower-pollen into her eyes, it is strange that as soon as it reaches them,
it instantly causes the eyes of her rival wife— who was already drenched in teardrops— to become clouded.
In this *kiṃśuka* tree, which has fallen into the middle [of its flowering season] and bears the form of a goad red with blood,
the splendor of the frontal globes of the elephant intoxicated by Love is now borne by her two breasts.

To her who has suddenly arrived here, this hospitality has been prepared by the *pāṭala* tree with its fragrant flowers— by that very tree which bears the burden of the imperial sovereignty of Kandarpa.
This woman, whose anger was softened by her beloved who offered salutations with joined palms,
now wipes away her tears with her fingernails and plucks a mango sprout from her bright face, as if she were uprooting her own pride.
These tresses of theirs, adorned with jasmine flowers, possess an indescribable beauty, like the spreading darkness of nights pierced by the rays of the moon, the beloved of the night-lotuses.
Having plucked flowers of various colors from the windows of the celestial chariot,
this youth fashions for her a crest-ornament as beautiful as a rainbow, which is truly worthy of her.

May I see the young bride, her beauty enhanced by vine-like arms and her waist losing its three folds like a slender creeper, as she plucks a delicate *madhūka* flower from the palace that rivals the luster of her own cheek.
"Make this flower of mine fragrant by imparting a drop of the fragrance from your lotus-face"—
thus does that *karṇikāra* tree seem to make this request, its creepers clinging to her hem.

Likewise, this fresh cluster on the mango tree has not attained such excellence of its own quality as that which exists upon the cheek of this lotus-eyed woman, marked by a line of black aloe-wood paste.
This Aśoka tree, struck by the feet of celestial beauties, bears its lovely limbs dyed with red lac,
as if Smara had placed a quiver upon its shoulder after issuing his unimpeded command over the world.
I believe that after a long time, this bakula tree has finally attained its desirable perfection;
for it has produced a flower for her, surpassing even the sprouts of the celestial trees of the gods.

The full fruit of her tenderness has finally been attained by the śirīṣa flower, which, having cast aside the blossoms of the celestial trees, has been worn as an ornament by this lady with long eyes.
As she placed a campaka flower to her ear with a hand marked by a pearl bracelet, this sweet-voiced bird did not offer her a blessing of well-being with its cries. (PNc 14.65)
With a bandhūka flower and a plantain leaf placed upon her face, the vine-like streak of *kālāguru* paste, moist with perspiration,
shines like a crescent mark on the moon, suspected to be a fragment of the twilight glow.
These women, their paths to the celestial chariots blocked by one another and failing to reach the flower atop the creeper,
become heavy with envy upon their rounded breasts, which have become burdensome to their slender-limbed bodies.

Behold, behold how these fresh sprouts, used as ear-ornaments by women with their lovers, see their own attained splendor as if it were their very selves reflected in the jeweled mirrors of their cheeks.
Whatever fragrant flower was found in the forest, that very thing was gathered by the women,
as if to fashion a bow for Smara to conquer the entire triple world.
Behold, on all sides, the beauty of the season has blossomed upon the limbs of these fawn-eyed women, who have made young shoots their ear-ornaments and are radiant with various floral decorations.
As drops of perspiration moved across their cheeks, as if offering a gift of pearls to the God of Love,
this fatigue of the fawn-eyed women began to embrace their slender limbs like a lover.
The faces of these women, marked by large beads of perspiration, provide a festival for the eyes,
like golden lotuses bristling with inlaid pearls.
Behold these lotus-eyes of women, their beauty of eyelashes obscured by the pollen of fallen flowers; through exhaustion, they are somewhat closing into buds.
[VAR 14.73b: {sauṣṭhavāni/ lem / em;
sauṣṭhavāni /ed}] Excellences.
Behold how exhaustion becomes manifest upon the vine-like arms of these Vidyādhara women, as their playful jeweled bracelets sink down and rest against the base of their wrists.

Just as the floral ornaments of these women, who are like clusters of blossoms from the wish-fulfilling tree of the bodiless god, are an infallible mantra for the Flower-Armed One, their jewel-ornaments do not shine with such brilliance.

"O King, these women are unable to leave the edge of the forest, which abounds in many flowers; for how indeed can that region be abandoned where there is such a dense proliferation of blossoms? (PNc 14.76)

Thus, even when his brilliant flower-like words had become guests of his ears, the king, smiling, became dejected; for he wondrously recalled the playful charms of the daughter of the lord of serpents.

Then, leaving behind that entire forest— which was a circle of flowers, sprouts, and shoots, and where rows of tinkling celestial chariots were adorned with golden bells— the army of the Vidyādhara king marched forward.
Now, the description of the Gaṅgā: She possesses a playful smile in the form of shimmering foam that kisses her bimba-like lower lip of coral;
she is adorned with a girdle of the rows of vocalizing swans, and her rounded hips are the banks covered in lush vegetation.
With its rows of waves turned tawny by the flickering radiance of golden creepers on the banks shaken by the wind,
the river appeared as if the saffron from the lovely breasts of the daughters of the serpent kings had been transferred to it as they sported and submerged themselves.
With the dark streams of rut flowing from the temples of the elephants of the quarters submerged within it,
the river appeared as if stained by the creeping smoke of the fire from the third eye of the Destroyer of Tripura.
Under the guise of the mass of waves splashing upon its shores,
the earth, as if on guard, seems to support hundreds of pillars made of sun-stones at its base, which are situated upon the hoods of the serpent-king bearing the world’s weight.
With one half of its body darkened by the dense shadows of the tall rows of *tamāla* trees rising from the bank,
it possessed a splendor like that of the Snowy Mountain, appearing as if it were the single embodied form of both Umā and her Lord.
With its clearly visible lotus stalks tossed about by female ruddy geese being pulled up by the beaks of male kadamba birds,
the river appeared as if jagged with the sprouts of crescent moons drawn from the peaks of the matted locks bound up by the fierce goddess Caṇḍī.

From afar, the holy city was beheld by that king, its beauty enhanced by chowries as radiant as the breaking of waves, and with a golden lotus parasol raised aloft; it appeared like the triple-pathed river Gaṅgā.

Then, on her shore— where the golden sands were washed white by the foam of the waves— a Vidyādhara established a military camp for her, while she was being gazed upon with smiles by throngs of women who were weary from the fatigue of gathering flowers.

Thereafter, that king, marked by his valor, entered a pleasure-pavilion suddenly prepared on the sandy bank by the Vidyādharas; in that pavilion made of white gems, the gazelle-eyed women were reflected both inside and out, creating the illusion that they had been carved into the very eyes of the structure.

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Gazing upon Pātāla," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* composed by Padmagupta—also known by the name Parimala—the son of the illustrious Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Fifteenth Canto:
Then, his forehead-mark (*tilaka*) moistened by thick drops of perspiration, he proceeded.
The people with dark eyes descended into the river water, which was as beautiful as a golden lotus, in order to bathe.
"Come, dispel your fatigue with the playful sport of impetuous embraces in my waters"—
thus, as it were, did the Ganges speak to the far-sighted ones through the cry of her flock of swans.
The fatigue of the women was forcibly dispelled by the breeze from the Mārutas, which was fragrant with the nectar of lotuses shaken by the wind and cool from breaking the waves.
With the women standing on the shore in rows that were clearly visible,
the river of the immortals bore a certain splendor, like a golden creeper growing upon its bank.
Upon a lotus petal that stole the luster of a dark gem— the very eye of those with white eyes—
the daughter of Jahnu bore, as it were, a half-moon of fresh pearl under the guise of a large drop of water.
As if overcome with modesty by their graceful and languid gait,
the rows of swans suddenly abandoned the sandy banks of the celestial river and departed for the breasts of the beautiful women.
The reflections of lotus-eyed women were captured in the waters, which resembled mirrors made of white gems, upon walls coated with white chalk where the figures of lovely damsels had been drawn.

Then the women entered the water, which possessed a garland of waves tawny with the pollen of golden lotuses blooming in the midst of the stream, while they placed their own sprout-like hands, with fingertips resting upon those of their beloveds, into it.

Having plunged into the waters of the celestial river, as if established in religious observance, the Sudarśana city immediately fell silent through its jeweled anklets, whose rays flickered like waves.

Then, through their playful sport in the water, the women with graceful brows attained a likeness to the amorous dalliance of Rati’s lover, even though the leaf-patterns on their breasts were washed away and their pearl necklaces had slipped from their threads.

Whom would the water, struck by the jar-like breasts of young women as red as fresh saffron, not cause to turn crimson? For what weak man would not undergo a transformation when his limbs are playfully touched?
Scattering water held in her jeweled horn while laughing, one woman approached from behind; with eyes half-closed in a sidelong glance, she repeatedly looked at her beloved with her neck turned.
[From behind]
Another woman, her arms raised high as they were turned back by the fullness of her breasts,
performed the beating of a drum in the water with her dangling, jingling jeweled bracelets.
Marked with the saffron from the jar-like breasts of the women of Hṛtapura,
the golden girdle shone upon the hips of the deer-eyed women like a loosened, undulating creeper.
Seeing her lover sprinkling water upon the face of another woman—
a face wonderful with its incessant drops of tears— a certain weak woman closed her own eyes.

Struck by the hands of the dense waves of the celestial river, the pearl necklace of the lotus-eyed women quickly snapped; for how can there be safety for the virtuous within the midst of the dull-witted?

She shone with a certain young girl who held a pure stream of water in her hand-like machine, like the playful bow of the one whose emblem is the sea-monster, from which the white flower-arrows have been released.

A certain lover placed a lotus-fiber bracelet upon the sprout-like hand of the fawn-eyed maiden, [a hand] which served as the abode for the moon— the god of love who dwells within the confusion of her halo.
Another woman, her breasts marked by fresh nail-scratches, covered them with a lotus leaf out of shame, while they were still wet from being washed with sandalwood paste applied by her lover’s hands.
On all sides, the moon-like face of the woman took on the luster of a cluster of stars;
in the water struck by the breasts of young women agitated in play, there arose a mass of bubbles.
The bride placed her eye upon the petal of a lotus, which was marked by the jeweled bracelet slipped from the tip of her own hand,
resembling a fragment of a cloud containing a rainbow within its circular interior.
The water did not carry away the mark of black collyrium from the eyes of those noble women with eyes like blue lotuses;
for that which dwells on the bank cannot effect the cleansing of stains adhering to others, however pure it may be.
The clear breath, agitated by the surface of her hips as it was overtaken by trembling waves,
momentarily took on the graceful appearance of a garment, like a mass of foam from the dark-lotus-eyed woman.
On the chest of the Sudṛśī woman, which was clearly marked with fresh nail-scratches and smeared with liquid saffron,
the sprout-like rays of the shimmering, large pearls of her necklace covered the eyes that had been fixed upon her lover.
With her locks of hair moistened by clinging water, the fair-browed woman rolled upon the edge of her forehead as if to behold the splendor of her eye, which was like freshly applied collyrium.

A certain woman, whose breasts were as round as gourds resting upon the surface of lotus stalks placed across her shoulders, attained a certain charm as if she were the lute of the amorous god’s play.
Another young woman, mistaking them for pearls fallen from her necklace broken by the impact with the water, fixed her gaze upon the drops of water in the hollows of lotus petals.
With eyes white in their centers, trembling and rolling out of fear,
those whose glances were like garlands of blue lotus petals wandered for a long time in the water together with the *śaphara* fish.
With their armlets fallen, their heavy jeweled earrings crushed by the great waves,
their golden bracelets slipped off, and the knots of their jeweled girdles loosened, the beautiful-eyed women shone forth.

The water of the Ganges, violently trembling with its waves and curved brows, reddened by thick, fresh saffron, was cast aside by the palms of women and appeared as if it had become possessed of rising anger.
Smara, whose bow was drawn into a circle, set his foot upon the women whose water-drenched braids were disheveled by their broad hips and whose cheeks were mottled with drops of water.

The water, shimmering with the rays of fallen jewel ornaments that formed a circle like a rainbow, variegated with flowers upon the hair, and inflaming the passion of the bodiless god of love, shone brilliantly for those fair-eyed women.
Then, with their hands adorned by single-gold lotuses, they emerged from there together with their lovers, who were skilled in repeated endearments, like the goddesses Śrīs themselves.

With their limbs made radiant by the luster of wet garments, the deer-eyed women— overwhelmed by intense shame born of that brilliance and adorned with the ornaments of clearly visible fresh nail-marks— delighted the eyes of their beloveds.
Then, wearing garments as white as the autumnal moon,
they performed their adornment upon bodies that were like golden creepers growing on the banks of the celestial river.
Marked with *tilaka* ornaments, emitting the fragrance of abundant flowers,
and bearing fresh, graceful leafy creepers, the deer-eyed women bore the charm of a grove of the God of Love.

Before long, the women shone like the utterances of the preeminent poets: they were exceedingly graceful, their delight established by particular ornaments, possessing ever-new charms that were to be perceived, and pure.
A certain woman bore a face as lovely as a silver lotus, upon which deer-marked musk-paste was delicately painted on her stainless cheeks, resembling a row of bees in its dark, silent beauty.
Upon her ear, she took a single golden leaf— a petal from the young tree of the God of Love— whose interior was as enchanting as an emerald with upward-reaching rays.
And a certain lady with eyes like those of a *cakora* bird placed her hand— marked by red lac and possessing a sweet, passionate luster suitable for kissing the face of her beloved— upon her lover.
Another woman wore a necklace as beautiful as the moon, its form woven with many bright gems; it was not only lovely upon her heart, but also kindled the fire of the god of the uneven arrows.
The gazelle-marked-faced woman placed upon the center of her forehead a tilaka made of thick musk-paste, like the footprint of an elephant rutting with passion.
Upon her hand, whose fingers were like petals budding with the luster of a hundred-golden lotuses stolen away by sleep,
a certain woman placed a jeweled bracelet fashioned by her other hand.
When the needle-like rays of emerald from the center of certain girdle-strings had arisen,
the line of hair on the fawn-eyed women did not attain distinctness, appearing instead like the wick of the lamp of Love.
Like a lake with its essence, the deer-eyed women, agitated by the flower-arrowed god of love, assumed a beauty through their jeweled anklets which clung to their lotus-feet like a lover.
The women shone brightly with their creeper-like tresses, which bore white flowers and displayed the shimmering play of waves of darkness variegated by the mass of moonbeams.

The women beheld their lotus-like faces, with eyes steady [in joy], reflected in jeweled mirrors held by the lotus-hands of their beloveds— mirrors that rivaled the splendor of the full orb of the moon.
Then, suddenly manifesting an intense passion toward the wine,
the women turned toward it like a mass of radiance turning toward the sun.
In the clear sky of the minds of those with eyes like young blue lotuses, there slowly arose the moon marked by the deer of the mind-born god, expert at shattering the mass of the darkness of pride.

Then, with their lotus-hands— whose new golden buds were held fast by the petals of her reddish fingers— the women with eyes like those of the *cakora* bird shone intensely with the fragrance of thick honey.
In pearl-oyster shells that momentarily held fragrant wine scented with blue water-lilies,
a swarm of bees hovered with restless longing, as if depositing the mechanical engine of the god of love.
The circle of bees, shimmering with rays, rested upon the lotus-cups;
it shone like the single, risen golden-handled parasol of the Lord of Rati, held aloft by its dark handle.
Held in the hand by her beloved, it was accompanied by a few bees.
The mind of the discerning was rendered helpless and uncontrolled by her, like the wine of Varuṇa acting upon the bowstring of the flower-arrowed god of love.
As the honey was being kissed by those with faces full of passion, as if it were a lover,
intoxication became manifest in the hearts of the fair-browed women, and a thrill of horripilation appeared upon the surface of their cheeks.

The honey, with its shimmering waves of playful smiles trickling from the lovely faces of young women bent down for drinking, possessed a splendor as if made white by the mass of moonbeams reflected in the mirrors.

A certain woman, her cheeks flushed like the *pāṭala* flower and her shimmering silver earrings swaying, drank the offered honey-wine, which contained the reflection of her own face like a trembling moon.
The moon-faced woman, with her exceedingly red eye that possessed the splendor of a blooming dark blue lotus,
drank the wine from the goblet as she desired, yet she drank her beloved with her eye.
The bee attained an equal appreciation for the fragrance of these three:
the honey of the wish-fulfilling tree, the breath from the woman’s mouth, and the blooming blue lotus.
Having received the kiss upon the tips of their lower lips from those whose eyes were as long as lotus petals, the wine became agitated by their sighs, as if repeatedly performing a dance out of joy.
Then the women sang the *Navasāhasāṅkacarita*, whose composition of words was not overly clear, like a nail-mark impressed upon the heart with intoxicating liquor.
With her lower lip moistened by wine, the young woman— resembling a mass of nectar—
caused the god of love to sprout within the hearts of the long-eyed maidens, which were already softened by the essence of passion.

The youth first bestowed their affection upon the spring, the friend of Love, which shines with an intensely crimson luster for the welfare of beloveds; thereafter, they directed it toward the sprout-like lower lip.
Through the intensity of drinking the honey-wine that had shaken away their pride, the hearts of those wide-eyed women suddenly attained clarity, as did their vessels made of transparent gems.

The young men, full of intense passion, did not merely kiss their beloved wives— who were the source of the intoxication of the bodiless god of love and who wore dark lotuses as ear-ornaments— but they kissed the wine as well.

The dawn, with its rosy glow, brought about the simultaneous loosening of both the modesty and the jeweled girdles of women; likewise, the spring, with its honeyed sweetness, brought about the simultaneous loosening of both the bashfulness and the jeweled necklaces of the lovers.

Then, from the hands of the Sudarśas, intoxicated with passion, pearl-oysters with reddened white bellies fell upon the sandy banks of the celestial river; and so too did the glances of their beloveds.
Then the woman with intoxicating eyes bore a crimson hue— like fresh sprouts—
upon her bright cheeks and within her eyes, having drunk deeply of the wine of youth.

Upon those women, whose speech was charming yet indistinct, whose long glances were like eyes half-closed with intoxication, and whose creeper-like tresses were thick with shimmering, variegated flowers, the God of Love set his foot.
The drinking hall shone with hundreds of crystal goblets— filled with wine and resembling blue lotuses—
as if they were rows of mouths opened wide out of curiosity to gaze upon the playful movements of the women unsteady with intoxication.
Having entered the marshy banks of the celestial river, where the darkness was driven far away by the light of closely set jewel-lamps,
they then sat down gracefully upon mats of fresh golden jambū shoots together with their lords.
Bearing limbs that were tawny like streaks of lightning and possessed a thickly blooming fragrance,
the fawn-eyed women, clinging to the necks of their lovers, attained a beauty like garlands of golden lotuses.
Then, with necklaces slipping from their threads, armlets shattered, and earrings bent,
the festival of love for those intoxicating-eyed women suddenly blossomed in full bloom through their passion.

Then, upon the chests of their beloveds— which were variegated with various body-pastes and strewn with clusters of flowers from their loosened, swaying braided hair— those women fell asleep from the exhaustion of lovemaking, as if upon the flower-bedecked couch of the God of Love.

The breeze from the waves of the Jāhnavī—causing the golden lotuses to tremble, turning them brown with the contact of the pollen from their filaments, and inducing a dance in the celestial trees growing upon its banks—removed the heavy fatigue from the amorous play of those women who were overcome by lassitude; it was the cause of Kandarpa’s great audacity in his forceful conquest of the three worlds.

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Plunging into the Pātālagaṅgā," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita*, composed by Padmagupta— also known by the name Parimala— the son of the illustrious Mṛgāṅkadatta.
**Sixteenth Canto** In the meantime, the Pāṭalā reached the sandy bank of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā).
They place their sprout-like hands, marked by the letter of the bodiless god (Kāma), [upon their hearts].
There, she beheld a crystal palace reaching toward the sky, from whose jeweled neck-pieces the bow of Indra was being emitted.
At that gate of sapphire, crowded with golden canes,
she shone like a streak of lightning clinging to a cloud as it clings to the crescent of the moon.
Standing at the side of the lord of the earth, who was situated by a jeweled window,
Ramaṅgada beheld her as she was questioning some gatekeeper.
And he, seized with agitation, caused her to enter within;
and she became like a stick of nectar for the eyes of the lord of the people.
She instantly ascended the lofty palace of white stone,
as did the King’s exceedingly clear heart, which was like a sprout of joy.
She bowed down before the king, her necklace kissing the earth, as she was being led by him to the state of being a worthy recipient for the affection of taking Ramāṅgada’s hand in marriage.
Although addressed by the king himself, "Come here, come here,
Pāṭalā," she sat down beside his jeweled couch of play.
Having thus conversed with that Cupid of the earth, Pāṭalā,
her sprout-like lower lip variegated by the rays of her teeth, spoke as follows.
O Great King, is this form of yours— this stream of nectar for the eyes that vomits forth the beauty of the god of love once it has been sealed— truly well?
"How have you entered this ground that is so utterly impassable? To whom would this power of yours not cause wonder, being as it is so exceedingly marvelous?"
"O Lord, some Vidyādhara has been liberated by you from a curse"—such is the widespread rumor here; therefore, who indeed are you? Homage be to you! (PNc 16.12)
"O Indra among kings, by whatever quality you are seized, for the sake of that daughter of the lord of serpents for whom you thus suffer—ah! [it is a great thing]."
Then the Lord of the Earth, his lip as red as coral and the radiance of his teeth shimmering upon it, smiled and replied to her with these words.
O Pāṭalā, does the daughter of the Lord of Serpents perhaps remember us from time to time during her casual conversations with her friends?
What does Anaṅgavatī say, and what does Mālyavatī speak? Is there even a slight rumor about us in the city of the serpents?
Having delivered my words to the ear of the daughter of the king of serpents,
has Ratnacūḍa indeed effected the transformation of Śuka’s form?
"Why have you come, and why do you appear so withered?
Tell me quickly; my mind suspects that something has happened."
To him, whose heart was moistened by intense love, who had asked for the delivery of a letter,
Pāṭalā handed over a letter that kindled the god of passion.
Having said to him, "Recite this which has been received," the descendant of the lineage of Paramāra cast it into the hand of Ramāṅgada, which was raised up in eager anticipation.
Having then deciphered those letters written with musk upon a golden plantain leaf,
he recited them clearly before her in a distinct voice.
Śaśiprabhālekha,
residing on the shore of the celestial river in the presence of the lord of the serpents, sends this message from Mālyavatī to the moon of the middle world who stands in well-being.
O King, the very moment our friend was separated from you in the Vindhya mountains,
she was pierced in the heart by the god of love, like a doe struck by an arrow.
O moon among kings, your gaze, which everywhere pours forth nectar,
has become a spray of *hālāhala* poison upon Śaśiprabhā alone.
She cannot be consoled by any object whatsoever, O Lord,
except for the hope of union with you, who are as cool as camphor.

Under the guise of teardrops resting on the tips of her eyelashes, this [tear] of hers, which has benefited her vision by allowing her to see you, acts as if it were a single-stringed necklace for her eye.
With her pale cheeks and moon-like face scorched by the heat of love, she speaks with clearly visible streaks of tears resting in the hollow of her palms.
Where is this woman with limbs softer than even the śirīṣa flower and eyes reaching to her ears;
and where is this fever of love, harsh as the fire of chaff?
Our friend finds no relief upon this bed of coral, nor in a chamber of snow, nor upon a couch of moonstones.
The warm waves of her sighs lead her naturally red lower lip to a certain pallor, as if it were her circle of friends.
Having fallen into a state of restlessness, this large-eyed woman tosses about upon her bed of lotus leaves like a tiny drop of water.
Her body, tender as a digit of the moon and scorched by the fire of love,
seems to melt away under the guise of a continuous flow of perspiration.
She firmly imposes emaciation upon her limbs, which are as delicate as flowers,
just as one places a bowstring upon a flower-tipped arrow.
O son of Bali, this [fire] held within my heart, though it has been offered with *haricandana* sandalwood and quenched by your story—
which is as cooling as water drenched with moisture— does not attain extinction.
"Drawing his bow back to his ear, the bodiless god of love pierces her limbs with sharp arrows; without you, O King, some inexplicable state has arisen in my mind."
This young girl, possessing an exceedingly transparent heart and perfect circularity, turns away from the mirror of rubies and faces you instead.
Like the wick of a lamp, this lovely woman, resting upon her burnt-out fringe,
trembles here and there from the touch of the wind of passion.
This lotus-fiber bracelet on her hand, which steals the luster of the moon and is joined with exceedingly long virtues, bears you upon her heart.
In her heart, which is a mountain of the fever of love, the lotus leaf shrivels up despite its intense moisture, yet the sprout of your love does not.
A bracelet is moved back and forth upon her wrist,
while her inner heart has reached the ultimate state of emaciation because of you.
Even a delicate thing generally turns out otherwise when circumstances change,
since even a necklace of lotus fibers became a cause of burning for her.
Placed upon the slope of her breasts by tearful maidens, the *vānīra* shoots— pale as the ripened fruit of the *lavalī*— are a supreme burden.
Neither with sandalwood, nor with usīra-water,
nor with water-sprinkled lotus leaves, does her fever of love find relief.
Moreover, O Lord of the Universe, you are the presiding deity of this heart;
therefore, she perceives the entire universe as being composed solely of you.
Now, by the message brought by Ratnacūḍa,
which is akin to a mouthful of nectar, this [woman] has somewhat regained her breath.
Come quickly with speed, taking this golden lotus,
before our friend here ceases to breathe due to the torment of love.
Having thus heard the messenger's reply regarding the contents of the letter, the king,
his body breaking out in a dense thrill of horripilation, spoke these words to Pāṭalā.
O Pāṭalā, do you not see that just as this friend of yours has fallen into some indescribable and distressed state, so too have I? // PNc_16.48 //
Therefore, you should go to comfort that moon-faced lady;
as for us and these others here, we shall strive to bring back the golden lotus.
"O sweet-voiced Mālyavatī, you must speak thus on my behalf so that this task may not be in vain, just as my heart's desire intends."
Then Pāṭalā, having been given a message by the king to be delivered upon her return,
went quickly to the city of the lord of the serpent kings.
Then, announcing the departure of that lord of the earth, a drum suddenly resounded with a sound as deep as the roar of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Then,
as he roared, the vine-like arms of the Vidyadhara women— whose minds were trembling with agitation— became slackened from the embrace of their beloveds.
In some way or another, a certain young woman managed to part the sprout-like lower lip of her lord’s face, while another separated the breasts from his chest.
With a smiling face and eyes cast askance at her beloved, a certain woman slowly fastened her girdle, adorned with nail-marks, around her hips.
"When my ivory comb is broken, my friends will look at me;
what should be done here? another girl became somewhat agitated.
A certain woman, seeing her couch marked with footprints stained with red lac,
was laughed at by her companions who cast their eyes upon one another.
One woman picked up a ruby bracelet that had fallen from the tip of her hand,
as if her heart had been pierced through its center by the flower-bowed god of love.
The playful men drank in with their eyes the lotus-faces of one another, whose bimba-like lips were stained by kissing and whose eyes were reddened by staying awake.
Then he, the foremost of chariot-warriors, set out to go toward the city of Ratnavatī with his chariot, accompanied by the forces of the Vidyādharas.
Then, on the road, that one worthy of worship by the world met with the young serpent Rātnacūḍa, just as the sun meets the moon at the new moon.
The moon,
its sound echoing across the circle of the quarters, became his vehicle,
like an elephant with a continuous flow of rut, as if it were his own self.
The rays from the crest-jewels of the advancing serpent-army, acting like needles of light, performed the function of lamps for the king, dispelling the darkness before him.
Then, after some time, by means of continuous stages of travel,
he reached a forest where the breezes were fragrant with the embrace of flowers.
Having stood there before him, he dispatched Ramāṅgada as a messenger to request the golden lotus from the lord of the Asuras with gentle words.
And he reached the city of Ratnavatī, which was constructed as if fashioned from the very essence of the three worlds, featuring lofty palaces made of jewels.
Sent by his lord, who had girded himself for the sake of Rāma’s purpose,
he entered that city after leaping across the ocean moat, just as Aṅgada had entered Laṅkā.
"Who is this? Who indeed is this?"—thus was he gazed upon for a long time by the citizens with eyes fixed in wonder, as they exchanged such blossoming words.
In the palaces of sapphire, he beheld the daughters of the asuras,
like flashes of lightning amidst clouds dark as the tamāla tree.
Being drunk in by the crystal shells of the eyes of the city women, he,
a lion to the herds of elephants that were his enemies, reached the main gate.
Then, announced by the doorkeeper, that hero entered the assembly hall of the lord of the Asuras— a place crowded with warriors from many regions who were itching for battle.
The description of the Lord of the Asuras:
He sat upon a lofty crystal throne, dark as collyrium,
like a fresh rain-cloud upon the peak of the king of mountains, Himavat.
He bore two arms entwined with clusters of rays from ruby armlets,
appearing like two blazing fires of his radiant majesty.
With his chest, which had resisted the tips of the tusks of the lordly elephant of Indra,
he wore a swaying necklace like a swinging cradle for the Goddess of Victory.
Wearing jeweled earrings that dispelled the darkness surrounding them with their brilliance,
he bore them both together as if they were the sun and the moon held captive.
There he beheld Vajrāṅkuśa, the ornament of the hero’s vow, the life-breath of pride, and the goad for the worlds.
He occupied that golden throne pointed out by him,
which was variegated with the rays of various jewels, like the sun upon a peak of Mount Meru.
Making the faces of the quarters smile with the moonlight of his teeth, the Lord of the Asuras performed a hospitable reception for the messenger and spoke to him thus: *PNc_16.78*
"Aha! Some auspiciousness has brought its fruit near for us today;
otherwise, why would virtuous men such as you come to our home?"
That wondrous conduct of yours in the hermitage of the sage Vaṅku has been brought to my ears by means of my spies who approached you.
"Tell me now, joined as he is with these Vidyādharas,
what does our master desire for you as the fruit of this journey to Pātāla?"
Those like you are not employed by a king for a trivial matter;
does the serpent Śeṣa extend his hoods for any purpose other than supporting the earth?
Therefore, tell me why you have been sent here by the king;
for my own request for those who seek it has never yet proven fruitless.
With his lower lip divided by the pure rays of his teeth, which were like long paths of speech,
Ramāṅgada smiled and spoke to him thus.
O Lord of Asuras, it is true that among these pure words, moist with the essence of nectar, you alone are their source, just as the moon is the source of all lights.
"Have you recognized this god who is marked by rashness? Or who does not know Virocana, the lamp of the world?"
He is proceeding by this path, along which the mountain of jewels has been crushed by his chariot, to marry Śaśiprabhā, the daughter of the king of serpents.
"It is said that her father has established a bride-price consisting of a golden lotus; for that purpose, O Lord, we have been sent by you."
If you desire to form a friendship with this one who is marked by daring,
then bring the golden lotus yourself and offer it.
"Before the dust from his army obscures the radiance of your face,
extend hospitality to this lord of the earth with a golden lotus."
What else? "The desires of those who seek do not fail because of me"—let this very statement of yours be quickly made authoritative.
When Yaśobhaṭa had spoken these words of Vajrāṅkuśa while being glared at by the resentful soldiers,
the elephant-like Asura laughed with contempt and replied.
"Alas! Though you are indeed clever, fie upon you, for you appear like one who is simple-minded, since even you, a learned man, have uttered something inconsistent."
Where are you humans, poorly situated as masters of this earth’s distress?
And where is that moon-like radiance, which is fitting for the Lord of the three worlds?
A jewel among women ascends such a lap as this;
for the sprout of the crescent moon indeed delights upon the head of Hara himself.
Whatever jewel exists here in Pātāla, wherever it may be, I alone am its vessel; tell me, who are you?
This arm of mine, spoiled by the play of conquering Śakra, does not tolerate even the offering of a golden lotus to the king.
O Lord, though you are skilled in policy, why do you act solely for our misfortune? Are you dragging along a garland of long blue lotuses that is actually a string of black serpents?
Turn back from this very place; abide by my word.
Why are you prepared to cast yourselves into a pit?
"As long as these asuras, who are like oceans, do not abandon their bounds,
so long should you protect our lord by retreating to a great distance."
Go, therefore, and dissuade the king from his desire for a difficult conquest;
for how can those like you remain indifferent toward a husband who has set out upon a wrong path?
Or, if he possesses the power, why does he still delay?
Let him come himself to take the golden lotus from here.
"Let something else be born; let him instead become a guest of my sword's edge!
Having said this, the lord of the asuras ceased speaking, trembling with rage.
