Alas, you who scratch at your unbending arms within the belly of this subterranean cave, where the wind of nirvāṇa blows— why do you boast so?
I think this dense darkness in your mind, which does not distinguish between self and other, has resulted from your long residence in the underworld.
The husband who was formerly born from her— the one whom they call the eighth form of Hara, who consumes the oblations— was known on earth as Paramāra.
Having descended into that lineage for the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods, do you think, "Fie on this mortal! regarding Kaṃsa’s enemy, the Primordial God?
Like Lakṣmī to Viṣṇu, like Pārvatī to the wielder of the Pināka bow,
she was a wife worthy of the daughter of the serpent-king for that king whose emblem was the fish.
O Lord of Asuras, you cannot forcibly make her your own;
a magnet has no power to attract a needle made of jewels.
Why do you place your foot here on this path and thus soil yourself with injustice?
For those who walk upon the wrong path, their fortunes go further and further away.
That you did not offer the golden lotus to the protector of the earth—
I perceive that very act as the unhindered gateway to calamities for you.
When that lamp of the lord of kings stands upon the field of battle,
these warriors shall before long attain the state of moths.
Act in such a way that the moon-like faces of the women of your harem do not rest upon the beds of your sprout-like hands.
Let this city of Ratnavatī not become one where the lamentations of the women of the townsfolk— afflicted by grief for their deceased lord— and the sounds of music have utterly ceased.
"Come, fall at his feet—he to whom the golden lotus has been offered by the god. May the meritorious dust of his feet fulfill your desire and purify your head."
"Or rather, rise up with your brave warriors and stand before him;
this king approaches together with the hosts of Vidyādharas."
What else is equal to this lotus of your head?
The Lord himself will surely take up this golden water-lily.
Having spoken thus, Ramāṅgada emerged from the midst of the assembly and went into the presence of King Raṇotka.

Then, approaching him slowly, the lord of Mālava bore upon his face a frown like the night of destruction for the king of the Asuras, as he softly repeated those various words of the enemy of the gods.
Then, having gone there with the encircling hosts of the Vidyādhara warriors, that king surrounded the assembly hall of Ratnavatī’s city on all sides;
by this act, the lord of the Asuras—whose great audacity in conquering the manifest gods was well known—possessed a facial splendor darkened by fresh humiliation.

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Entreaty of Kanakāravinda," in the great poem *Navasāhasāṅkacarita*, composed by Padmagupta—also known by the name Parimala—the son of the illustrious Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Seventeenth Canto: Description of the Battle.
Then, while the city of Ratnavatī was being oppressed by the armies of the king of the Ahi-vidyādharas, the warriors—
boasting of the pride of their arms and filled with wrath— rushed forth, having drawn their scabbards from their swords.
Due to their mutual clashing, sparks leaped forth from their golden armor;
to whom did those flames not cause the suspicion that they were the seeds of the fire at the end of an eon?
Bearing terrifying frowns upon their brows and sword-blades with the luster of bees in their hands,
others went forth in wrath on clever horses that tore up the earth with the tips of their hooves.
And the host of elephants, their broad temples reddened by a thick flow of vermilion,
shone like a mass of great mountain peaks whose summits have been licked by a fresh forest fire.
In front of the jeweled archway stood that massed army of the enemy of the immortals, which had been blocked by the flood of the Vidyādhara hosts brimming with the intoxication of battle.
Then that great lord of the asuras, mounted upon an elephant, his bow-staff raised with pride and a pair of quivers fastened to him, went forth with speed like Egoism incarnate.
Deep and resonant like the roar of clouds at the end of an eon, the sound of his battle trumpets rose up;
echoing intensely and most terrifying, it filled the interior cavities of the netherworld.
Then those heroes, possessing the luster of fine lotuses and heaps of collyrium, impelled by him, swiftly dispatched their elephants and swords against the enemy ranks on the path of victory.

A battle broke out between the great serpent-lords, the sovereign Vidyādharas, and the foremost Asuras, filling the sky with sprouting garlands of flames issuing from their swords as they struck one another.
While the heroes were charging, the elephants moving unrestrainedly, and the horses leaping about,
the seven nether worlds trembled, fearing that the end of the eon had arrived before its time.
Displaying their prowess with weapons while being longingly gazed upon by celestial nymphs,
the warriors began, as it were, a most marvelous dance in the midst of the stage that was the battlefield.
Leaping with speed along the path of the wind, the heads of the elephants— smeared with the water of rut— were swiftly split apart by the Vidyādharas using sharp saws of sword-blades.
Falling upon the frontal globes of the great elephants— which were emitting a dense spray— and resonating with a sharp clangor,
the polished scabbards of the preeminent Vidyādharas shone like loud bursts of laughter released from pearls.
The discuses abandoned by the former gods found their way into the ranks of the Vidyādhara armies, which were crowded with the coils of sword-blades acting like undulating waves.
Upon the hoods of the serpents that had fallen upon them—hoods rough with worthless jewel-stones—the great asuras, though wielding swords, became softened; yet their desire for battle did not.

The sounds of bowstrings, the lion-like roars of asuras delighted by those strings, the neighing of horses, and the trumpeting of elephants— having issued from the openings of their caves, they flowed forth upon the earth and filled the depths of the netherworld.
The dust raised by the earth of jewels, kicked up by the hooves of the galloping cavalry,
overspread all the faces of the quarters of the sky, marking them with the luster of Indra’s bow.
The earth of the battlefield became terrifying, as if strewn with thousands of young sun-disks, by the footprints of elephants filled with warriors' weapons and thickened by their own rutting ichor.
Severed by the thousand-fold sword-blades of the great warriors along with their roots, and drenched in sprays of blood,
the flapping ears of the elephants bore the likeness of the frantic palm-leaf fans of Yama.
The arms of the warriors, severed from one another with great force, fell at first with the luster of nails copper-red from the new dawn;
they appeared like lords of serpents, complete with their crest-jewels, falling simultaneously as if struck by a single glance.
As streams of blood flowed profusely from his limbs pierced by swords, spears,
and arrows, he plunged into the mountain ranges of the world-system like elephants entering the cascades of flowing red chalk that trickle down in sport.
Thousands of heads of weapon-bearers, severed by swords upon the earth,
shone like lotuses uprooted from the midst of the battlefield-lake by Time.
The flock of herons, flying over the heads of the headless trunks from which blood was gushing,
appeared for a moment like the parasol of Death, with its staff made of blazing, crimson jewels.
With the multitudes of sky-dwellers departing and the circles of elephants' frontal globes falling,
the sky displayed a resemblance to the orb of the sun as it descends upon the vast slopes of the sunset mountain.
In an instant, the army of the lord of the asuras— its foot soldiers falling, its horsemen crushed, and the trunks of its rutting elephants severed—
was destroyed by the vidyādhara troops along with their heroic elephant-riders.
With elephant-ear conch-shells fallen on all sides like swans from smiling riverbanks,
the deep river of blood suddenly began to flow with surging waves.
While the great asuras were fleeing, their fortitude snatched away by the predatory warriors among the Vidyādharas,
the son of the enemy of the gods, named Viśvāṅkuśa, then entered the battlefield in his chariot.
With arrows drawn back to his ear from his bow and shaped like crescent moons,
he alone turned the brave warriors of the enemy army away from the field, just as one turns cowards away.
From the hands of the Vidyādharas, whose own excellence had been eclipsed by his prowess,
there fell sword-blades that resembled tears mixed with drops of water, for pearls were released from the frontal globes of elephants struck at their tips by the edges.
Then, in an instant, the forces of the Vidyādharas and the Pannagas were routed,
like the waters of rivers overwhelmed by the ocean swollen by the full flood of the moon's rays.

The son of the serpent king and the lord of the Vidyādharas were unable to obstruct his course, just as the great mountains Mahendra and Sahya cannot withstand the irresistible force of the ocean rising at the time of universal dissolution.
Then, commissioned by the king to remove the itching of his staff-like arms,
Ramāṅgada, with his bow drawn at the front, went swiftly on his chariot to the path of battle, his brows arched like creepers.
Thus, the increase in the roar of him who was about to engage in battle with the one born of the reeds (Kārttikeya) was perceived by the teardrops falling upon the cheeks of the wives of the Asuras.
From afar, Yaśobhaṭa, with his chariot, checked with a succession of arrows the son of the enemy— who was well-armed and charging headlong with great speed— just as the son of Indra checked Karṇa.
Then Viśvāṅkuśa released a golden arrow at his chest, which was protected by an excellent armor;
it struck him on the slope of that great mountain whose body was dark as collyrium, like a cloud discharging a torrential rain upon a mountain of shining peaks.

The chariot of Yaśobhaṭa, though he was filled with fury, revealed the joy of the Asuras' delight through its aimless aiming, releasing, and falling— its driver swooning, its horses struck down, and its very form reeling.
Then the son of the enemy of the gods severed with an arrow the girdle of Kālarātri, which was the path of the rising wrath of Antaka, as well as the bowstring of Ramāṅgada.
With his navel-mirror possessing the great splendor of a broad expanse, and with the shimmering anklets of the Goddess of Heroism,
he too— like Viṣṇu against Rāhu— seized him and severed his head with his discus.
Then, in the sky, a host of beautiful Vidyādhara maidens danced while their anklets tinkled;
and they showered a rain of celestial flowers upon her head, where the jewel from the weapon that had crushed his skull lay.
When he saw his own son’s head blown off and the armies fleeing in all directions,
Vajrāṅkuśa rushed toward his father like the sun toward the mountain of setting.
Rushing forward in battle, his elephant, showering ichor and adorned with a golden girth,
shone like a cloud dark as a *tamāla* tree driven by the wind and flashing with lightning in the midst of the sky.
Drawn by the rope of their lord’s gracious smile, the warriors turned back and stood before him;
eager to sacrifice their own lives, stained with the prospect of defeat, at the front of the battle.
Having mounted the lordly elephant, who was as delightful as the moon ascending the sky and adorned with a garland of stars,
the king Navasāhasāṅka then set forth to subdue his enemy, the darkness.
On one side was the lord of the Vidyādharas named Śaśikhaṇḍa,
and on the other was Yaśobhaṭa, who was like a unique cool-rayed moon to the forest of lotuses that was his enemy’s army.
Even that young serpent prince Ratnacūḍa came before him, his darkness shattered by the mass of light from the jewels in his flickering hoods and parasol-like canopies; his valor was not in vain.
The remaining forces of the Vidyādharas and Pannagas, their swords brandished and their bows drawn into circles along with their arrows, fled before him.
Amidst the rising *aṭṭahāsa* laughter of *vetālas* who clapped their hands while intoxicated by the blood of their enemies,
that battle between the great warriors proceeded with total disregard for their own lives.
Upon the heads of the weapon-wielders, the sword-blades falling against one another shone like garlands made of blue lotus petals, playfully cast by the celestial nymphs.
Some bore armor that possessed a beauty here and there like fresh red-pink lac,
as if marked by the juice of the lac-dye from the lotus-feet of the playful Goddess of Victory.
A certain anguish arose within the enemies from those arrows that had entered their hearts but remained impure—
just as the wicked experience distress when they encounter the virtues of the virtuous, which have already begun to bear fruit before them.

The dust of the powder from the weapons of swords clashing against one another, falling in streams and possessing the luster of *tāpiccha* blossoms, took on the grace of the collyrium smoke for the playful dalliance of the Goddess of Victory.

For the beautiful wives of the enemies of the gods and the Vidyādharas— who were terrified by the horrific clamor arising from the destruction of both armies— the two states of grief and joy became like a swing.
Then,
blinded by rut, the lordly elephant of the Asura king, with its upraised stream of ichor, rushed impetuously into the midst of the battlefield and struck the Lord of the Middle World.
There, from the crests of the two great elephants, the fire produced by their tusks created,
for a moment, leafy vines of gold upon the sheaths of their trunks, which were tawny with the sparks of their counter-strikes.
As his bow was being drawn tightly again and again by the lord of the people,
a deep *kreṅkāra* sound arose like a roar of defiance during the undertaking of the slaughter of his enemies.
The arrows discharged by him of vast prowess, their feathers rubbed by his quivering earrings,
fell upon the chest of the enemy king— upon that chest where the decorative leaf-patterns on the breasts of beautiful women had been wiped away.
Then, as sparks of fire flashed forth from the armor released by Arāti,
the form of the lord of the earth shone as if it were a mass of sparks from the fire of his own prowess issuing outward.
The golden row of the earthly king’s arrows shone intensely upon the exceedingly high head of the great asura,
like a garland of rays from the sun clinging to Mount Añjana.
Rising up, the trail of dust from the sapphire armlets shattered by the arrows of his enemies appeared like a streak of smoke from the fire of valor residing in his mighty arms.
Ramaṅgada, knitting his brows, struck down the enemy’s heroic warrior who stood at his side and was skilled in weapons;
with his arrows, he scattered the demon’s banner of victory like his fame, white as moonlight.
With his bowstring severed by the arrows released from the bows of the foot-soldiers of Uḍḍāmaravairin stationed below,
that long-armed hero hurled discuses like the bracelets of Kālarātri.

Leaping up, the lord of the Vidyādharas, who had effortlessly struck down his adversary facing him, also cut with his sword the golden staff of the enemy of the gods' banner— staff which stood like a pillar of victory for the world over that haughty foe.
In that same manner, Ratnacūḍa crushed the frontal globes of his enemies' elephants with his *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon,
such that the spray of pearl-dust rising from them attained the state of a white parasol for him.

The fearless Indraśatru, bearing a lofty and harshness, marked the pair of frontal globes of Śrīsindhurāja’s elephant with crescent-moon wounds, as if making them into a pair of breasts for the Goddess of Victory.

On the field of battle, the pearls from the elephants, stained red with blood, shone brilliantly; they created the illusion of falling sparks of fire as they were cast off when the tips of their tusks struck one another.
Whichever arrow the enemy of the gods, his eyes clouded with anger, hurled at Pṛthūtilaka,
the mighty-armed king shattered each one in mid-air with his own arrows, as if destroying the very hope for victory.
The Goddess of Victory, having rejected both Karṇa and Arjuna through the excellence of their respective bows,
moved back and forth between them like the surging tide between Mount Suvela and the ocean.
Then the lord of the Asuras seized the mass of rubies from the crowns of his subjects' husbands,
just as the wind at the end of an eon sweeps away the spreading clusters of jewel-flowers from the wish-fulfilling tree.

Then, out of anger, with an arrow whose brilliance rivaled the crescent moon, Navasāhasāṅka severed the head of the enemy of Vāsava— along with its dangling jeweled earring upon his thick shoulder— just as Rāma severed the head of Viśravas’s son.
Then, the faces of the quarters in every direction resounded with waves of noise from various musical instruments,
and a garland made of celestial flowers, released by the wives of the enemies of the Asuras, fell upon the head of the God.

The broad pair of arms of the Lord of Lakṣmī— his prowess being beyond all mark— shone as if marked by the fresh and dense impressions of the bowstring, yet unmarked [by blemish], as if stained by the lac-dye from the lotus-feet of the vanquished and powerful Fortune of his enemies who had approached him with great reverence.

Before him, women with eyes like those of Vidyādharas, serpents, and deer, their cheeks adorned with streaks of saffron stirred by the striking of golden earrings, sang auspicious hymns of victory in voices resonant with deep, surging joy.
Smiling, with the bow-staff placed in his hand by Yaśobhaṭa and having cast off his jeweled armor,
the lord of the sky-goers wiped his face with the hem of his garment, where droplets of perspiration appeared like bursting pearls.
Then, having entered Ratnavatī, where hundreds of citizens who had sought his protection were presenting him with offerings of jewels,
he consecrated that young serpent prince in the kingdom of his enemy— a prince whose essence of heroism had been clearly proven in battle.
Taking that golden lotus from the grove like a personified heart’s desire along with its stalk, the king—
eager to obtain that jewel because it was said to belong to the daughter of the lord of the earth— then set out for Bhogavatī.
The impetuous king reached that city, whose festivals could be inferred by the deep resonance of drums, which seemed to prop up the earth on all sides with its lofty jeweled mansions,
and which was smiling with the mass of pure luster radiating from the hanging pearl festoons that swayed upon the tips of the crests of its exceedingly high jeweled archways.

Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Seizure of Hemakamala," in the *Navasāhasāṅkacarita*, a great poem composed by Padmagupta—also known by the name Parimala—the son of the illustrious Mṛgāṅkadatta.
**The Eighteenth Canto: The Vision of the King of Serpents**

Then Śaṅkhapāla, the lord of serpents, his joy surging deep within him, went out to meet the king who had arrived—the very essence of whose strength was evident by the three worlds he had made his thorn—bearing in his hands priceless gems as offerings. Thus ends Canto 18.1.

Having accepted the *arghya* offered with reverence by the Lord of Serpents and having stationed his army just outside, that god, worthy of the *arghya* of the virtuous, entered the city with humility,
preceded by the crest-jewels from the necks of the lords of the Vidyādharas.
Abandoning their songs before they were finished, interrupting their graceful dances, and suddenly casting aside their jeweled lutes from their laps,
the women of the city rushed to the windows, their minds intensely agitated by the curiosity to behold him.
Lifting with a trembling sprout-like hand the jeweled and pearl lattice-work at the top of the window,
he looked out with a smile, his eyes playfully curved like the playful spray from the crest of a sea-monster.
As that moon among kings rose, a certain woman, with a graceful curve of her hand like a rising wave, cast glances toward him—
glances that were like friends to the variegated waves of water from the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) and the celestial river (the Gaṅgā), and which were like yawns of passion bursting forth.

Having playfully cast a handful of fresh pearl blossoms upon him, a certain long-eyed woman, her jeweled bracelets jingling and her gaze fixed on the king whose shoulder she had struck, what indeed did she not do out of modesty?

Beholding that moon among kings, whose chest was as broad as a slab from the mountain of the immortals and whose arms reached down to his knees, another woman’s body bore a thrill of horripilation upon the weight of her breasts— a thrill thick with the bliss of an embrace brought to mind by her heart.
Seeing him reflected in the surface of the mirror, a certain girl, thinking "I have caught him," became filled with joy;
but when that image passed before her, the innocent girl, whose moon-like face was distressed by the sight of the empty void, became despondent.

Thus that royal swan moved about amidst the minds of those fawn-eyed women— minds which were like lakes shimmering with waves of ever-new passion— as they fell under a succession of Love’s arrows, their girdles loosened by the twisting movements of their limbs.
In the music hall, we have constantly heard the glories of this king sung by the celestial bards of the Lord of Serpents;
that very King Navasāhasāṅka has now, by our merits, become the guest of our eyes—oh, how wonderful! (PNc 18.10)

May this Lord, the lamp of the lineage of Paraśurāma, who has overspread the horizons with the radiance of his splendor, be victorious over the worlds; for he has now utterly uprooted the mass of darkness belonging to the enemies of the gods, establishing light upon the surface of the earth.
Indeed, he is the sole boat for crossing the ocean of the overwhelming burden of the serpent king’s incomparable vow;
and he is the ripened fruit of the longing that has long held its place in the heart of the daughter of the serpent king.

Having quickly fashioned from the hand of Yaśobhaṭa that golden lotus as a playful crest-ornament, upon which sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree are inlaid, this king shall today take the hand of Śaśiprabhā.

Hearing these words of the citizens, which betrayed their intense devotion, he beheld before him the lofty jeweled temple of the Moon-crested Lord, renowned as the illustrious Hāṭakeśvara, which was like an axe for his enemies.
Having entered there, he bowed down once and worshipped the Primordial God with flowers produced from the wish-fulfilling tree;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he began to offer praise, his speech blossoming with the rays of light from teeth as white as *kuṭaja* flowers.
Homage to you, O Bāṭu, who, though dwelling within [the body], has the river of the gods hidden inside; whose eye is the concealed command of the arrow;
and who is skilled in the jesting that discerns the true nature of the Daughter of the Mountain, who was exhausted by her severe vows.
Homage to you, whose lotus feet are inlaid with the manifold rays from the crest-jewels of the gods and asuras bowing with extreme devotion;
homage to you, who possess hands made awkward by the twilight salutations of Pārvatī, who feels jealous as she rests upon half of your body.

Homage be to that [Lord] who, for the sake of the great sun that has been utterly consumed by fire, always performs the task of producing the sprouts of jewels from the skull-cup moistened by the water of the leakless ocean upon the head of you, the destroyer of worldly existence; salutations to him!

Salutations to you, the well-flowered one, who subdues the pride of Kandarpa; the destroyer of Death (Kṛtānta); the creator of auspiciousness; who is encircled by the lord of serpents; whose lofty body consists of the earth, wind, sun, moon, fire, water, oblation, and ether.

Salutations be to you, who are white with unbroken ashes, whose body is enveloped in the skin of a lordly elephant, who have swallowed serpents, who have consumed the race of Dānavas, whose sole purpose is the destruction of calamities, and who are the cause of all that is praised.

Obeisance to you, whom those who know the Self declare to be the very shore of the ocean of speech— the sacred syllable *praṇava*— and who abide within the lotus of the heart, opened by the hearts of great sages absorbed in meditation.

Salutations to you, who wear the crescent moon as an ornament; whose mountain-like matted locks resound with waterfalls from the sky like waves crashing against skulls; who are pure with ashes as your body-unguent; and whose crest-jewel is the moon among the serpents that serve as your blooming sacred thread.

O Lord, salutations to You who indeed possess that unmanifest form, wherein there is neither weapon, nor ashes, nor matted hair, nor a garland of skulls; neither the moon, nor the river of the perfected ones (Gaṅgā), nor a necklace of serpent-kings; neither a bull, nor poison, nor even a beloved wife. PNc_18.23.
Having praised the journey of the Naga King, the Lord of Avanti departed from that temple with his companions;
he went to the palace of the serpent king, where emerald pedestals were set within and the female Nagas moved about.

Having descended there from his chariot with the hand of Ramāṅgada supporting him, he entered gracefully upon a floor of polished ruby set with a profusion of thick, blossoming flowers, amidst the rising sound of auspicious musical instruments.

Then, in that place, he beheld the assembly of the serpent kings gathered together upon magnificent golden thrones; they were established in their positions, praising one another’s blossoming victories, while the lotus-petal eyes of Padmacchadāya looked upon them.
Once he had passed from the range of vision, the assembly of serpent kings, with hands joined in reverence, immediately offered him the honors he deserved;
like the Mandākinī river, it became filled all around with golden lotuses in bud by the glances of Hariṇāvacūḍa.

He of noble lineage offered his salutation to him, whose splendor was formed by the luster of the jewels on the hoods of that [serpent], which were joined by the mass of light from the rubies shining in his downward-hanging crest-ornament, and whose footstool was kissed by the gems in the crowns of kings.

Having left behind the crossroads strewn with women and studded on all sides with gems, as directed by the lord of serpents, he of the broad shoulders respectfully ascended the golden throne situated in its center, upon which a venerable, aged hooded serpent had offered his blessing.
Having slowly dismissed Vatsa with the words, "Go to your own kingdom," the Lord of Serpents sent Ratnacūḍa to the chamber of sapphire in the inner apartments;
there, he had two seats prepared for him and for Yaśobhaṭa, the lord of the Vidyādharas, at his side.

Then, upon a golden throne, with the darkness shattered by hundreds of jewel-lamps and a white parasol, he sat down not far from the Lord— the sole ornament of the three worlds, who had torn asunder the enemy of Indra.
Standing to one side and listening there to the auspicious songs of young women, that deer—whom Yaśobhaṭa had previously seen on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains—stood as if fixed in a painting;
then, smiling with wonder, he was pointed out by Yaśobhaṭa to the king.
In the meantime, the king, his eyes rolling with joy, beheld from afar Śaśiprabhā approaching— the daughter of the serpent king,
slender and with a form as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, like the bow-staff of the god of love.
With her moon-like face bathed in the glow of white silken garments like moonlight, wearing ear-ornaments of fresh barley sprouts recently grown by her mother,
and having cast off her radiant wedding attire including the charming festive bracelets, she bore a dress suited to the occasion.

Bearing on her cheek, pale as a *lavalī* fruit, a decorative leaf-design of black aloe-wood that was so exquisitely beautiful it raised the suspicion of being a single wreath of smoke from the fire of love painted by some friend, she stood there.

Bearing a body suffused with loveliness, she was like the presiding goddess of the milk-ocean of erotic passion— a source of self-adornment, a chamber for the play of the bodiless god of love, a means for performing graceful dalliance, and the ultimate limit of a festival for the eyes.
Fanned by the breeze from the *pāṭala* flower whisks, her creeper-like tresses slightly disheveled, she walked with her friends;
moving slowly out of modesty, she took steps whose tinkling anklets were not very clearly audible.
With her eyes— whose lashes were raised, whose lotuses of playful charm were surpassed by the expansion of incomparable and radiant joy,
and which were parched by the intense fever of love— the heroine too drank in the king from afar with the cupped hands of her eyes.

When she had approached her father, who was seated upon a golden throne, her lotus-like face bowed with modesty, Mālyavatī spoke thus to the Lord of Mālava at the conclusion of the appropriate honors performed with garlands and other offerings: *PNc_18.39*
O King, O moon of the earth,
why do you delay?
Even now, with this [wealth] acquired by your own arm, act quickly!
Having fashioned for her an ear-ornament from a golden lotus, fulfill the vow of the Lord of Serpents.
When she had spoken thus, Kamalāvataṃsa placed that golden lotus upon the tip of the ear of the daughter of the serpent-king;
at that moment, abandoning his noble deer-form, he appeared before her as a man of majestic stature, holding a golden staff.
Questioned by the king— who was filled with wonder and longing— as to who he was and how he had become a deer, he,
his body being drunk in by the succession of the serpent’s eyes, spoke these words to the Lord of Avanti.
This is the account of the gatekeeper:

"I have been cursed by the sage Kaṇva, who was provoked by the denial of entry at the door due to the obstruction of Giriśa, whose abode is Mount Kailāsa; I am this very Pratīhārapāla of your father, the illustrious King Śrī Harṣadeva."
"When King Navasāhasāṅka places the golden lotus of the daughter of the lord of serpents upon his ear,
you shall regain your own form"— thus did that great ṛṣi, having offered his conciliation, decree the end of the curse.
"Having gone to the mountain Ekapiṅgala, I shall crown you with this fame born of victory over Vāsava’s enemy.
Having said this and scattered divine flowers upon his head, he departed for Pātālamalla by way of the wind.
While the sounds of musical instruments resounded and bards recited loudly, that protector of the middle world was led by the priest of the Lord of Serpents to the sacrificial altar,
upon which a water-filled jeweled pitcher was suspended from a corner, accompanied by her.

In that city, Mālava-puṣpaketu duly married the daughter of the serpent, whose ear-ornament was a golden lotus darkened by streaks of smoke released from a fire with rising flames— just as Kuvalayāśva married the daughter of the serpent.
Having been brought there, she of a form never before seen, with her limbs rippling like waves of the flower-arrowed god of love,
shone as he met her— just as Śantanu did upon meeting the digit of the moon from the netherworld in the river of heaven.
Holding in the palm of his hand something covered by a cloth, which was filled with the luster of shimmering sparks,
the Lord of Serpents spoke thus to him, the radiance of the gems in his lips being variegated by the upward-shooting rays of his fangs.
O King Navasāhasāṅka, there is nothing such as that which is being given to you here in my house;
for they declare you to be one who has surpassed Purandara in sovereignty, possessing hundreds of treasures established in your treasury.
Therefore, take this single crystal Śiva-liṅga, fashioned with the skill of Tvaṣṭṛ, which is as pure as your own self;
for within it, those of meritorious deeds behold the form of the Ancient Foe (Śiva) possessing the body of a woman who is half his own.
In ancient times, it is said that Vyāsa received this from the sage of the Purāṇas; from him, it is said, it passed to the palm of the hand of the primordial poet (Vālmīki).
From him, the venerable great seer Kapila obtained it, and by his grace, it has been bestowed upon me.

Having spoken thus regarding the offering of the Śiva-liṅga, the king— having suddenly subdued his enemies— took up that priceless and most purifying object, which had been offered by the Lord of Serpents and in which the singular form of Śiva was clearly manifest, as if it were his own glory condensed into a single mass, possessing the luster of the full moon.

Then, there arose a certain festival of sound, with the tinkling of the restless anklets and waist-bells of women moving along the edges of the quarters, and the rising clamor of drums, flutes, *huḍḍukkās*, conchs, lutes, *mṛdaṅgas*, and *murajas*.
Then,

when the great festival of the wedding had taken place, that king, eager and having turned back the lord of serpents through his respectful pursuit, set out for his own city, taking with him his daughter-in-law, who was a banner of incomparable prowess.

Then, having traveled a great distance from the abode of the serpent, that portion of the Ancient Person emerged effortlessly with his army along a path where the mass of water was suddenly parted by the majesty of Śiprā placed before him.
Having offered the guest-water (argha) with his own hand by the assembly of sages, he set foot upon the shore of the ocean all at once;
and at that moment, the Blessed One, the kinsman of the lotus, possessing the reddish glow of a bandhūka flower, stood upon the peak of the Golden Mountain.
Entering Ujjayinī,

he entered the city which was offered handfuls of flowers by the citizens, as if it were conversing with him through the exceedingly sweet cooing of the pigeons perched upon the turrets of the palaces bathed in the morning sun. PNc_18.58.

Then the ministers, who had fallen into a state of emaciation through their very anxiety for him, paid homage to that descendant of Kakutstha, who was joined by his beloved wife and the illustrious Śatrughna,
and who was followed by the son of Sumitrā and the daughter of King Janaka, as if he were the slayer of the enemies of the gods himself.

Having met them halfway on the road, his eyes moist with tears of joy at the sight of Mahākāleśvara, he spoke to them with a smiling face and proceeded with them toward the abode of the Destroyer of Tripura, which was made enchanting by the resonant ringing of golden bells struck by the hands of Vidyādharas and Uragas.
Having performed the ritual worship according to tradition for Hari— the crest-jewel of the crown of the Teacher of the moving and the unmoving— at that place,
he entered the royal palace together with the daughter of the Lord of Serpents, amidst the waves of the sound of conch trumpets that filled the sky.

Having stayed there for some days amidst the sound of ocean-like drums and the festive blare of trumpets, that moon among kings, whose lineage was thus adorned, departed for Dhārā— the royal capital of his family— as he heard from his ministers the history of how it had been obtained.

Then, as the city windows were opened by the beautiful women of the city out of curiosity to gaze upon him, the capital became like a woman with wide-open eyes as the Lord entered after a long time, as if he were her very life-breath returning.
Then, having attained its consecration, he of priceless character had that Śiva-liṅga made of crystal and jewels installed there;
and the Vidyādharas performed its worship with blossoms from the blooming wish-fulfilling trees, fashioned by his supernatural power.

Having performed the customary and sincere rites of farewell at the conclusion of the festival, he then sent both— the son of the lord of the Vidyādharas and the son of the king of the Nāgas— back to their own country, his hand placed upon their shoulders as they stood with the jewels of their crowns loosened from their temples due to their stay in the temple.

One of them went to the mountain of moonstone, which was marked by clouds parted by an army moving through the sky; the other also went to his own capital, which possessed a broad highway granted by the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā) with its unfathomable waters.
"O friend of Śaśiprabhā,
never turn your face away from Rāma, for compliance with his will is the supreme means of intoxicating him.
Having spoken thus to that daughter of the serpent, the daughters of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Mahoragas, and Siddhas departed for their homes.

Then, the Goddess of Imperial Sovereignty— adorned with a dark parasol and her pale cheeks marked by the patterns of musk-paste from the hand of the daughter of the Lord of Serpents— was playfully placed once again upon the long arm of the King, that preeminent minister who had long held her, the arm where the scars from the striking of the bowstring were still growing.
Now, the eulogy of the work:

Padmagupta—whose exceptional poetic genius was attained through devotion to the illustrious Rājendra Śaladaṅka Rāma, the beloved friend of poets; whose splendor is like that of a lotus blooming at dawn—has composed this account of the life of the noble King Sindhurāja. (PNc_Gp.1)

O Lord of the Earth, who is the ever-springing vine of the goddess Lakṣmī; O Sindhurāja, who are the jeweled mirror for the playful display of knowledge—wear here upon your ear this earring of a ruby, fashioned by me from this poem of radiant luster.
O Navasāhasāṅka, these few drops of the nectar of eloquent speech which were bestowed upon me by that divine friend of poets— their splendor now shines forth like pearls bathed in moonlight.

O King Navasāhasāṅka, whatever slight impetuosity has been thus set forth by me, dull-witted as I am, the cause here is solely your command—which has laid low the crowns of fierce kings like flowers—rather than any pride in my poetic skill. (PNc_Gp.4)
Thus ends the Navasāhasāṅkacarita in its entirety.
